## v80 — Session 759 — The gates by school, first slice: goblins are a gate's state, not its kind (Michael's A, §9a)
Michael's A of Session 754 made each old gate one of the six schools, and goblins *a state any gate can be in: a quiet or spent gate that a goblin warren has moved into* (lore_canon Part II §9a). Backlog C carries the build for both builders. This session takes the piece that is fully specified and the systems builder's: the *occupied* flag, replacing the goblin theme.

`gateOf(entry)` (`20-quests.js`, beside `THEME_DEF`) reads a gate's stored theme. Anything but *goblin* is its school as before. A gate that drew *goblin* (the world's roll, an authored entry such as *The Last Post*, or an old save, all read the same way) is an occupied gate of one of the five built schools, the school picked by a hash of its seed. `makePortalDef` takes the school as the portal's theme and sets `occupied`. So the gate is lit, fogged, scored and furnished as its school (`THEME_DEF`, `DUN_DAMP`, the rooms, the music, the glow all key on the portal's theme), and two lines in `56-dungeon-build.js` read the flag: its floor takes the warren's junk, and its foes come from `OCCUPIED_ROSTER`, the old goblin list (Goblin ×2, Kobold Thief, Slime, Cave Troll, Shieldbearer). The stored word stays *goblin*, so the gate's name (*The Black Den*, *Godou Burrow*) and the townsfolk's *goblins nest there* still read from it, unchanged.

Nothing is re-rolled: the world's draw is the same, and the share of goblin-held gates stays at one in six. Gaoth is not among the schools an occupied gate can be until it is built (its look and its foes); adding it then moves about a sixth of the occupied gates to another school, which changes only their look. The test harness's `enterDungeon({theme:'goblin'})` builds a portal by hand and still gets the old goblin look; nothing in the game does that.

Each school's own roster against the canon's table is a rule of play and Michael's: asked as **DECISION #252**. Under the table read strictly, a level-one character in a Cloch or Scáth gate would meet only the Skeleton fallback, so the options keep a first-level foe in each.

## v80 — Session 762 — The health bar keeps the stretch a blow just took; the bottom centre stops saying the blows you take (#198 A, second slice)
Session 761 put the blows you land at the foe's head. This session does the other half of the same answer. Under Michael's A on DECISION #198, combat lines stop, and the prototype (`docs/prototypes/hud/`, auto/concept) shows a blow you take as *the pale stretch your health bar has just lost (kept 0.8 s, then it drains)*. The bar's new paper is the look's; the tail works on today's bar, so it is built here.

`hpTailStep(frac, now)` (`62-actions.js`, beside `updateHUD`) keeps the tail where the bar stood before a loss. It holds for 0.8 s from the last loss, then drains at half the bar a second until it meets the bar. A second blow inside the hold restarts the hold, so a flurry reads as one long stretch, and a heal past the tail takes it along. `updateHUD` sets `#hbt`, a cream strip (#efd9b8 at .8) behind `#hb` in the same bar, in `index.html`. It watches the bar, not the blows, so a trap, a fall, a burn or a ship's volley shows the same.

The lines it replaces are gone:
- *Bandit hits you for 7!*
- *🛡 Blocked! Bandit hits for 3 (reduced)*, with its hints *— equip a shield for better protection!* and *— Steel Claymore hafts the blow*
- *Archer's arrow hits for N!*
- the Faolchú's *🔥 … fire hits you for N!* and *🛡 Resisted! …*
- the dungeon caster's *Magic bolt hits you for N!* and *🛡 Resisted! Magic bolt …*

A block still flashes blue and sounds; a parry still flashes gold. *… strikes empty air.* on a roll stays: it is a dodge, not a blow taken. A guard break says so as before. The sea's archers' line is in `85-world-sea.js`, the look builder's file, and is left for them.

- a loss from 1 to .8 holds the tail at 1 through 790 ms, reads .9 at 1,000 ms, and stops at .8

## v80 — Session 768 — A new look, shown: a from-scratch render slice of the Gatelands (prototype only)
Michael asked what the kept concept art becomes, and how the game stops looking like Minecraft and starts looking like a modern game. First, a survey of how the game draws itself: 774 boxes, 273 cylinders and 122 cones among its shapes, 522 Lambert materials against 13 standard ones, no tone mapping, no post-processing, three.js r128 from 2021, and flat fill light (ambient .55 plus hemisphere .55 against a sun of 1.15).

The first attempt kept the game and changed only how it draws (`docs/prototypes/render/`, `newlook.js`). It added linear colour, ACES, ambient occlusion from depth, bloom, haze, a grade and a Kuwahara filter, plus auto-smoothed normals that also blend the per-corner colour jitter `mergeParts` gives every crown and rock. The jitter, not the shading, is what makes the crowns read as facets. The smoothing helped most, but the result was still recognisably the same game. Michael stopped it: he wants a complete reimagining.

The second attempt is new code, `docs/prototypes/levelup/` (`main.js`, about 410 lines, three.js 0.170 vendored from npm because the CDN is blocked here). It renders one view aimed at key frame 2 (OG-077):
- the sky: a gradient dome and 2,051 cloud puffs in lit heaps;
- the land: a terrain shaded in its fragment shader (Voronoi fields with hedgerows, woods from afar, rock, sand, the path), on a grid dense at the camera;
- the near ground: 160,000 instanced grass blades and 5,200 wildflowers on one wind;
- the trees: 881 of them, made of leaf cards with normals turned out from the crown;
- the village: 80 cottages of plaster, thatch, slate, shutters and flower boxes, a church and a three-arched bridge;
- the Weaver ruin on its hill, a lighthouse, sails, and mountains with their own haze;
- the image: physically based light, a 4096 shadow map, bloom, a warm-and-cool grade and ACES.

Two views: the hero vista (`hero.jpg`) and the riverbank at eye level (`village.jpg`, `?view=village`). It is not wired to the game.

Also this session: the five routine prompts that should read backlog L were written out with their additions (Session 767's ask). Agents cannot edit routines created through the API, so they went to Michael as a paste page. The look builder's "section H only" lines were adjusted so they do not contradict the new paragraph. A decision is raised on whether to build the new foundation.
### Verified (headless Chromium)
`node docs/prototypes/levelup/shoot.mjs` renders each view in about 15 s at 1920x1080 in software GL, with no page errors. The counts in `window.__stats`: grass 160,000, flowers 5,200, trees 881, houses 80, puffs 2,051. The comparison page puts the slice beside OG-077 and today's paintover frames.

## v80 — Session 770 — People from a genome: MakeHuman's body, our wardrobe (prototype only)
Michael asked why the game's own genome system could not simply be raised instead of buying a hundred one-off meshes. A Meshy test confirmed the doubt: the download needs a paid plan, and the auto-rig fused the cloak to the arms. The answer built here keeps the genome and changes what it drives. The material is MakeHuman's base body, released CC0 by its makers in 2020, from their GitHub:
- one sculpted mesh of 19,158 vertices;
- the morph targets that reshape it, for gender, age, ethnicity, muscle, weight, height, proportions and 28 face and body sliders;
- a 163-bone skeleton with skin weights for every vertex;
- two fitting shells ("tights" and "skirt") that the same targets reshape.

`mh_pack.py` packs what the slice uses into one 7 MB binary (generated, not committed). `people.js` does the rest:
- **The genome:** a handful of numbers, mixed into target weights as MakeHuman mixes them.
- **The skeleton:** built from joints read off the morphed body, then posed: arms down from the A-pose, elbows and fingers bent, the jaw closed, the head turned.
- **The wardrobe:** cut from the fitting shells and pushed out in layers (trousers, boots, a tunic that hangs looser below the chest and cinches at the belt, a short or long skirt, a belt, cuffs). Hems are cut cleanly in the shader on the unmorphed body, so every garment fits every body, and the body's own skin is hidden under clothing.
- **Fur mantles:** eleven noise-cut shells.
- **Hair, beards and moustaches:** procedural hair cards rooted on the scalp, combed up and back, hugging the scalp and then falling, kept off the face, shaded by their root's normal. A shell cap with a smooth hairline sits under them.
- **Eyes:** with irises, set in the helper's sockets.

`people.html` shows a line-up of eight Markfolk and a close-up per face (`?view=faces&who=N`), and five of them now walk the village lane.

Corrections found on the way, for the record:
- binding the skins before the skeleton had world matrices doubled every offset (the first render was grotesque);
- three.js caches a shader by its compile function's source, so per-material cut lines and fur layers need their own `customProgramCacheKey`;
- the hair helper is a hair volume, not a scalp: hair rooted on it floats.
### Verified (headless Chromium)
The line-up (8 people), the faces and the lane (5 people) render with no page errors in 7 to 13 s. The live page's bundles load and run when served locally.
### Needs eyes
The faces at eye level, and the women's long hair, which is still untidy at the temples. Frame rate with many people on Michael's machine (the live page's line-up). The question Michael raised at the end of the session: a builder of our own, for creatures as well as people.

He left what clearing one gives to the quest writer, with a seed: it unsettles the world and draws Varek's ire, the Elder Scrolls' Towers inverted. That is now in `lore_canon.md` §9a and backlog A. Michael then set the shape of the two paths (13 Oct). Varek's path brings power and corrupts the world, gate by gate, until the sixth unmakes it; Varek turns at the last gate and dies trying to stop the player. The other path restores the world at a cost to the player's magic, and Varek opposes it. This is recorded in `decisions.md`, `lore_canon.md` §9a (with a note on the Act III outline it overrides in part), backlog A, and the foundation brief, which plans the corruption's look as one level read by the grade, the sky and the trees.

## v80 — Session 772 — Creatures from parts: one kit of skeletons, one gait engine (prototype only)
Michael asked whether there was work to start while Sessions 768–771 sat in CI, and where to lean in. He pointed at his own idea: a skeleton for every creature type, as MakeHuman gives the people one. Claude's answer was to build skeletons from parts rather than one per species. The bestiary is about a hundred and twenty animals and monsters, and they fall into about a dozen body plans that share their pieces. The game already half does this: `wolfSkeleton` bends one 24-bone rig into a wolf, a boar, a bear, two horses and the dragon with flags. Michael: "yes, write it up and start the creature prototype"; and while it was built, "Be mindful that there are several other animals / monsters that are on other concept art files."

**The kit** (`docs/prototypes/levelup/creatures.js`, three.js 0.170 like the other slices):
- **Parts:** a spine, a neck, a head (skull, muzzle and jaw, with eyes, ears, horns, antlers, crystal horns, a beak and fangs as rigid bits), a tail (with a curl, so a scorpion's tail is one number), arms on any socket of the spine, wings (an arm and a fan of fingers with a membrane skinned to both edges), spines down the back, and leg pairs over eight presets: canid, ungulate and plantigrade fore and hind, bird, insect, sprawl.
- **Presets:** a preset is joints in the leg's own frame as fractions of its height, so one preset fits any size.
- **Flesh:** grown, not modelled. Tapered capsules on the bones make a field; capsules of one limb join hard and parts join smoothly; surface nets mesh it at a cell sized to the thinnest limb, and Taubin smoothing takes the steps out without shrinking the body.
- **Weights:** the skin weights are read off the same field, so a joint bends where the flesh joins. So are the tones, the counter-shading the game's wolves already use, the patterns, the fur mask (noise-cut shells, as on the people's mantles), and the binding's glow (a seam down the spine and cracks over the hide).
- **Gaits:** one gait engine for any number of legs. A gait is a duty factor, a Froude number (speed against leg length, so a giant walks like a giant), a stride, and a rule for each foot's phase from its pair and side. *Walk* (a wave from the back) is a quadruped's four-beat walk, a hexapod's wave and a biped's walk. *Trot* (alternating diagonals) is a trot, an insect's tripods and a spider's tetrapods. *Gallop*, *slither* and *fly* complete the set.
- **The solver:** analytic. It yaws an insect's coxa toward its foot, holds a paw or hoof, bends the two segments between them, and slides the leg's root toward the foot past its reach, as a shoulder blade does.
- **The genome:** `{plan, seed, sliders, tint, light}`, about 150 bytes, with six generic sliders (size, leg, bulk, neck, tail, head) that act on any plan. The seed comes from a key of place and index, never `Math.random`.

**Ten plans, all from the concept art:** the Ironwolf, the Faolchú (the wolf's plan with the canon's extra arms out of a red spine seam, and cracks), the Frostreach Bear, the Elderstag, the Shatterhorn and the Mineprowler (both six-legged: Michael's 9 A), the giant spider, the Stormplume, the dragon, and the Mire Snake. `bestiary.js` and `creatures.html` show them in a line at true size, each beside a 1.8 m figure on a floor ruled in metres (`?view=line`). One creature walking (`?view=one&plan=…`) has a panel to change the gait, roll a seed, move the sliders and read the genome. `?bones` shows the skeleton through the flesh.

**The catalogue, by plan** (Michael's call-out): every animal and monster on the sixteen sheets that hold any is sorted into fourteen plans in `character-builder.md`. Ten plans are prototyped; two parts are owed (fins, radial chains); the human rig takes the goblins, trolls, skeletons and wraiths; and the slimes, elementals, golems and wisps need kits of their own.

Corrections found on the way, for the record:
- the palette was read as linear colour and every coat came out pale;
- a straight leg cannot reach the ends of a real stride, so the feet fell 3 to 8 cm short until the root could slide;
- the line-up's spacing missed the horns and wings until it measured the whole creature.
### Verified (headless Chromium)
`node docs/prototypes/levelup/creatures.check.mjs`, all passing with no page errors:
- Builds: all ten plans, 18 to 69 bones and 8,600 to 84,500 triangles each, in 0.04 to 0.93 s.
- Weights: every vertex's skin weights sum to one.
- Feet: every foot reaches its target at 48 points through every gait of every plan (worst under 0.1 mm).
- Duty: the share of the stride a foot is down matches the gait's duty (a wolf's trot 0.45 of 0.45, a spider's walk 0.71 of 0.68).
- Genomes: about 150 bytes.

`--shots` writes `creatures-line.jpg` and one picture per plan, flesh and bones.
### Needs eyes
- The creatures walking live on Michael's machine: whether the gaits read as animals (the wolf's trot, the spider's tetrapods, the Shatterhorn's slow wave), and the frame rate with fur.
- The faces close up, which are soft, as grown flesh is. Sculpted targets or image-to-3D heroes are the answer where it matters.
- Whether the parts' approach is the one he wants before the kit moves to the builder's page and then into the game behind the foundation's switch.


## v80 — Session 773 — Creatures from parts: the bound, the hop, the sideways walk, the pincer (prototype only)
Michael, on Session 772's line-up: "They all look great! Should we go ahead and tackle more of the skeletons? This framework seems to be working very well." The catalogue table names what is owed, so this session takes the gaits and the claws, Session 774 the swimmers and the radial bodies, and Session 775 the shells and feathered wings.

**The kit** (`creatures.js`):
- **Flights:** a gait's flights, the stretches with no foot down, are found by sampling the stride once per gait. The body follows a ballistic arc through each (h = g t² / 8 at the top), and the swinging feet rise with it. The trot and gallop of the older plans gain their small real suspensions this way.
- **Two gaits:** the *bound* (hinds together, then fores, the spine flexing) and the *hop* (every foot at once). The hop is a pulse: the body covers only the stance's short sweep while its feet are down and the rest in the air, so `step` now reports how far the root moved (`C.moved`) instead of a constant speed.
- **Two leg presets:** a hare's hind leg (a long foot from the hock) and a frog's (a Z).
- **Headings:** a plan may walk at a heading in its own frame (the crab at 90°); the same feet and solver walk it sideways.
- **The pincer:** an arm with a swollen hand and two fingers. Also eye stalks, and a throat sac that fills and empties.
- **The saddle:** the first thing hung on a socket for a rider, set on the fur, not under it.
- **Scale:** a plan may stand at a multiple of its parts (`scale`).

**Five plans:**
- the Snowleap Hare;
- the post hare of OG-077, which is the hare's parts at 5.5 times with a saddle (three lines);
- the Bellthroat, a red frog with its violet sac, hopping;
- the Dunescorpion: four leg pairs, pincers and a stinging tail;
- the Tidecrab, blue, walking sideways.

The line-up now holds all fifteen, sorted by height as built.

## v80 — Session 774 — Creatures from parts: fins and radial bodies (prototype only)
The second of the three sessions Michael's "go ahead and tackle more of the skeletons" set going. Session 772's catalogue table named two parts the kit lacked: fins (fish, whales, rays) and radial arms (octopus, squid, jellyfish, the Wisp). This session builds both.

**The kit:**
- **Fins:** a thin sheet on a bone of its own, so the pose can flutter it. The outline is drawn in the fin's own plane: a *tri* for a dorsal, pectoral, pelvic or anal fin, a *fork* for a tail. A fork upright is a fish's tail; laid flat it is a whale's flukes. A fin hangs off the spine at any t, or off the tail's end. All of a creature's fins are one double-sided skinned mesh.
- **Radial arms:** chains from a ring round a centre, each sinking and bending by a number of degrees a bone, kept off the floor where they lie on it. Thick arms are flesh, so the smooth union webs them where they meet. Thread arms are thin tubes with an HDR colour that blooms.
- **Three footless gaits,** paced in body lengths a second (`bl`) with a stride of 0.7 of the body, whose length the build now measures:
  - *swim:* a wave from head to tail, growing toward the tail, with the pectorals fluttering. A whale's (`swimAxis: 'x'`) runs up and down.
  - *crawl:* a ripple round an octopus's arms.
  - *drift:* a jellyfish's bell beats, closing at the rim, while its threads trail.
- **The page:** a water surface over a swimmer. The camera now frames a creature that hovers, not only one that stands.

**Four plans:**
- the Riverjaw Salmon, red for its run, with seven fins;
- the Storm Whale, 14 m, with long flippers and flat flukes;
- a giant octopus, eight arms webbed into its mantle and lying out across the floor;
- the Wisp of OG-018: a blue bell that glows, four oral arms and fourteen glowing threads, floating 1.5 m up.

Corrections found on the way, for the record:

- **The soar:** a gait for a bird aloft. It lifts the body to the plan's flying height, tucks the legs up under it, and beats the wings.

## v80 — Session 776 — The Makers' tools, the frame; a reload no longer launders stolen goods or unseals a quest piece (Michael's B on #175)
Michael chose B on DECISION #175 on 6 Oct: six tools, one for each god with a shrine (`docs/design/unique-artifacts.md`). Nothing had been built since. The page's build order starts with one session for the frame and a suite. This is that session, and it adds nothing a player can meet yet. `87-world-quests.js`, after `anchoredPlaces`, now holds `ARTIFACTS`: the six tools under the page's working names, each with its god's `GODS` key and its check (the Gate-Blade Might 30, the Sundial Ring Swiftness 30, the Wolf-Mother's Cloak Resolve 30, the Shuttle Intelligence 35; the Drowned Bell and the Waylamp have none, because the tide and an honest week are their trials). `artifactPlaces()` picks where the two home-island tools lie, as `anchoredPlaces` picks Caer Slige. The Gate-Blade goes to a Gatelands gate, a ruined gatehouse when the island has one. The cloak goes to a Gatelands lair that is not a story place. Each is drawn on `seededRng('artifact', id)` from candidates sorted by id, so every machine gets the same pick. The other four are placed in their own sessions. `artifactCheck(id)` reads the attribute's base plus at most 2 from gear (`ARTIFACT_GEAR_MAX`), so a Fortify ring closes a small gap and no one buys Might 30. `artifactTry(id)` takes the tool when the check passes. When it fails, nothing is lost: the try is kept in `worldState.artifactTries`, the character's key (`SS_CHAR_WS`). The shared state changes only through two named actions (the co-op rules). `takeArtifact(id)` writes `worldState.artifacts[id]` (the world row) and puts a `unique` item in the bag. `yieldArtifact(id, to)` takes the item from the bag, the stash or your hands and records who now has it. Both keys are on the S242 list. The Journal's Quests view now opens with *Things not yet yours*: one line for each tool you have tried and not taken, in the menu voice, with its number (*The Gate-Blade — Dunmore Tower. Might 30.*). This is a fix, not a new rule: each mark now does what its own session said it does.

## v80 — Session 777 — The Wolf-Mother's Cloak: the beasts let you be, and its town pays (the Beasts' row of #175 B)
The second session in the page's order, the Beasts. This one builds what the cloak does and what it costs (the page's Beasts row), and leaves the trial for later. The cloak is now a real item: `ARTIFACTS.wolf_cloak.item` makes *The Wolf-Mother's Cloak*, worn on the back (def 1, weight 2), drawn as the fur cloak until it has a look of its own, unique and never sold. Its rule is `beastAtPeace(e)` (`87-world-quests.js`). While you wear it, Wolves, Dire Wolves, Snow Wolves, Cave Bears and Spiders (`CLOAK_BEASTS`; never a boss) leave you alone unless you strike first. A beast that has lost health to you is marked `_struck` for good. The open world's foe tick drops such a beast out of alert and skips its sight check (`42-zone-enemies.js`), and so does the loop's dungeon pass (`90-main.js`). `alertPack` wakes a calm beast only when the one calling is a beast you struck, and the woken one then stays awake. So hitting one wolf brings its pack, and a Bandit who sees you does not bring the wolves beside him. The cost is the page's: the beast lives, so the town nearest its lair loses 0.6 prosperity a day while the cloak is yours and the master alive (`cloakDrain`, in `tickProsperity`'s flag effects, kept in the fraction as occupation's half point is). The drain stops when the master dies or the cloak is given up. The live lair's own −0.6 a day on nearby towns was already there and is unchanged.

Not built here: the trial (Resolve 30, walk into the den and leave without killing the master; the den is a look-builder piece), and the Fighters' Guild's way (kill the beast and the cloak comes off its corpse *worth half as much*). What *half as much* means for a cloak whose virtue is a peace is not settled. It is asked as **DECISION #263**, together with approving the quest writer's *The Makers' Things* as the tools' words, which every trial needs.

## v80 — Session 780 — The Gate-Blade's key: a gate you have walked opens to it (Michael's 3A on #263)
Michael answered DECISION #263 on 13 Oct with A on all four parts. This session builds the third, the blade's key. The page says the Gate-Blade *opens a sigil gate's door without the gate's key*, *only gates you have opened once*. Since Session 517 a gate has no key, so the rule he chose is this: with the blade in your hand, a locked door inside a sigil gate you have been down before opens at a touch, and no pick is needed. The game kept no record of the gates you had walked (`wdisc` marks a place seen from the road, not entered). So `noteGateWalked(portal)` (`87-world-quests.js`), called by `goToDungeon` as you go down, writes `worldState.gatesWalked[seed]`. It reads whether the gate was there before it writes, so a gate's first visit is never one the blade opens. Lair caverns and the tutorial crypt are not sigil gates and are not written. The key is the character's, where you have been (`SS_CHAR_WS`), and is on the S242 list. E at a locked dungeon door (`interact`, `50-travel.js`) asks `gateBladeOpens(door)` first. If it holds, `gateBladeOpen(door)` opens the door as a picked lock opens (the mesh goes, the cell becomes floor, the unlock sound plays). This is the co-op rules' one named action for the change. The first time, it says the approved draft's line, *The Gate-Blade goes into the lock as if it were cut for it.* (kept in the character's `stats.bladeKeyed`), and after that *The lock gives.* With any other blade in hand the door is picked as before. Moved #263 under Answered in `docs/decisions.md`, with what was done.
### Verified (headless Chromium)
`tests/bladekey` (new), 9 of 9, in the fixed gate 42 (one locked door on its first floor). The blade was taken at Might 30 and held. On the first visit E at the locked door leaves it shut (the cell still 5) and asks for a lockpick, and the gate is written as walked, `{42:1}`. Out and down again, E opens it (the cell becomes floor, 1) with the draft's line. Locked again and touched again, it opens with *The lock gives.* With an Adamant Longsword in hand instead, the same door, locked again, asks for a pick. `gatesWalked` rides the character row and not the world row. A lair cavern's portal and the tutorial's are not written. No page errors. Neighbours green: `gateblade`, `makertools`, `lockfair`, `chestpicks`, `coopsaves`, `corpsebody`.
### Needs eyes
A save made inside a gate on its first visit carries the gate as walked, so after *Load last save* there the blade opens its doors. The rule's *opened once* is generous by that much. Dungeon doors have no ids and are not saved, so a door the blade opened is locked again on the next visit and opens again at a touch. Whether the blade wants its own sound at the lock, not the pick's unlock, is the look and sound builder's call.

## v80 — Session 784 — The Waylamp held: the lamp pays for the room, and an inn can have it back (the Hearth's row, in the approved words)
The second half of the Waylamp. Held as your own (`lampOwn`: the trial won, not given up, on you) and lit (`lampFree`), the lamp pays for any town inn's room. The room offer opens with the draft's line in the inn's people's words (*There's no charge to the one carrying that lamp. There never was, and I'd not be the first.*, *You've the lamp. No charge.*, *The lamp's bearer is not charged, Master. That is the custom, and the house keeps it.*, *The lamp pays.*), then gives the house's own offer as it stands. The draft puts the lamp's line first, so the house's price is still named, and the custom waives it. The answer is *Yes.*, not *Yes. N gold.* Taking the room costs nothing, the house answers with its own *made up* line for that room (*The first door on the left, made up already. …*), and the log says *the Waylamp's bearer is not charged*. While the lamp is out (Session 783's seven days), or in the stash, the room is paid as before. The page's other half, *any coach seat costs nothing*, has nothing to act on: the coach charges no fare (a seat is held for nothing, Session 237), so the draft's *(the lamp: no fare)* is not shown. The claim, the draft's *Give the lamp to the house.*, is at any town inn while the lamp is yours. `lampGive` gives it up through `yieldArtifact` (the co-op rules' named action): the lamp leaves your bag, hangs over that inn's door (`artifacts.waylamp.hung`), the town's favour rises by 2, and the log reads *Gave the Waylamp to The Salt Gate, at Biafaira.* The house thanks you in its people's words. The round can begin again from there: `lampHome()` is that inn now, where it was the first town's first inn. That inn offers *The lamp over the door?*, and *I'll carry it.* starts a new trial with that town not to count. The draft's rumour (*There's a lamp over the inn door at ${town} that burns in the rain. …*) is in `liveRumours` for the town whose inn holds the lamp and every town in the eight cells round it, while it hangs there. The coaching inn is in no town, so it neither lets a room for the lamp nor takes it.

## v80 — Session 786 — The Noon Ring: the weather turned once a day, and the lightning drawn close (the Sky's row, in the approved words)
The page's Sky row, its virtue and its cost. Used from the bag (`useItem` → `noonRingTurn`, `87-world-quests.js`), it turns the weather once a game-day, through the weather's own shift as `devWeather` does: clear to rain, or rain to clear, each with the draft's line on screen and in the log (☀). The same day it says *The ring will not turn again today.* Under any other sky (fog, snow, a storm, overcast), or under a roof, it says *The ring does not turn under this sky.* and nothing changes. The day it last turned is the tool's, in the world row (`artifacts.sundial_ring.turned`). The cost: while the ring is on you, the storm's lightning (`86-world-crime.js`, the weather tick) brings one flash in three down close (`noonRingFlash`). The ring is warm.* is said, and after that the log reads *Lightning, close.* Neither the page nor the draft says a close strike harms you, so it does not; the roll is cosmetic and stays `Math.random`. ### Verified (headless Chromium)

In fog and in a storm it gives the refusal and the sky stays. Of 3,000 storm flashes, 34.3% come down close with the ring and none of 300 without. ## v80 — Session 787 — The Gate-Blade's claimant: the Crown's gold and commission, or its twentieth (the Stone's row, in the approved words)
The page's last column for the Stone: who wants it. ## v80 — Session 790 — The Shuttle's claimant: the Church would have it under seal (the Weaver's row, in the approved words); a gift never skips a power's ninth service
The last claimant on the page, from the approved *The Makers' Things* (second run). While the Shuttle is on you and not given up, the Prior at the Compact's seat (the lord at Fortargent, `churchShuttleTopics`, `87-world-quests.js`, in both lords' topic lists in `83-world-generator.js`) asks *The shuttle.* in the draft's *la Navette* speech. *Give it to the Church.* yields it through `yieldArtifact`. With the Compact open to you, it enters three services. Sworn elsewhere (another power's rank of 2, or the Compact closed), it enters none, with the draft's *a clause, not a sentiment* line. Either way the letter to the Royal Herald is written: `artifacts.shuttle.herald` holds the day, for Aldwyn's thanks through Corwin, which is owed to a later session. The log reads *Gave the Shuttle to the Church at Fortargent.* *I'll keep it.* and *Not now.* change nothing. A priest anywhere offers *The shuttle.* at the top of the church's talk (`shuttlePriestTopics`, in the church's `_extraFn`), in the church's people's words. The Prior's pronoun follows the seat's lord (*Take it to him* at Fortargent, whose lord is a man), and the Aurennais line names the seat.
Building it found a hole that Sessions 787 and 788 share. A claimant's services were added straight onto the power's count, and the rank was read from it. So a gift could carry the count to nine and the rank to the third: Knight of the Gates, Captain or Prior. That skipped the ninth service, its finale and the war it starts (`warFromFaction` is called only at the turn-in). With three services at once, a Factor at six would have been made Prior by the Shuttle. One function, `giftServices(power, n)`, now enters a claimant's services for all three claims. They count, but never past the eve of the ninth service, so the finale is still played. A rank already at the top takes them all. A rank the gift raises is logged as a turn-in's is, with the power's name capitalised (*The Compact: named Clerk.*). The turn-in's own log line still opens lowercase (*the Compact: named …*); that is older and left alone.

With the Shuttle in the stash nobody asks. Fortargent's priest, an Aurennais, says *That object is the Prior's concern, Master, at Fortargent, and not this house's. I would take it to him. I would not keep it.* The four peoples' lines are the draft's, with *him*. The Crown's claim given at eight services leaves 8 and rank 2, with no war. No page errors. ## v80 — Session 797 — The Shuttle's trial: the deepest room of its gate, and Intelligence 35 (the approved draft, second run §5)
The page's Weaver row put the Shuttle *in the deepest room of the gate nearest the home island's last unread sigil*, and Session 782 left that room for its own session. It is built here. **Where.** Which sigil is *last unread* changes as you read, and for each player, so a place keyed to it could not be one Shuttle per world, the same for a friend in the host's world (the page's own rule and the co-op rules). So the gate is picked from the seed as the other tools' places are (`artifactPlaces().shuttle`). It is a home-island sigil cave gate, dry, not a fort, a lair or the Root, and never the blade's gate. In this world that is *Carrigbeg's Silence* (seed 818845). If Michael meant the gate to move with your reading, only the pick changes. **The room.** On the gate's lowest floor, the Shuttle lies at the open cell farthest by walking from where you arrive (the entrance, or the stair down). Among the cells within 85% of that distance, it takes the first whose eight neighbours are open, so it lies in a room and not at a corridor's dead end (`shuttleSpot`, `shuttleLay`, called from `goToDungeon` after the lair's master). **The trial.** The first time you come within four units of it, the draft's *Something small and pale lies on the floor under the sigil, the shape of a boat, or a fish, or neither.* is said, once (the character's `stats.shuttleSeen`). Within 1.4 units the prompt is *Press 'E' to take up the shuttle*. Below Intelligence 35 (the base plus at most 2 from gear, `artifactCheck`), E gives *You can see it, and you cannot see where it is. Your hand closes beside it every time. Not yet.* That costs nothing, and the try is kept for the Journal's *Things not yet yours*. At 35, *You pick it up the way you would pick up something you had put down a moment ago.*, and the log reads *Took the Shuttle from the deepest room of ${gate}.* `takeArtifact` and `artifactTry` take an optional log line for this. Their default stays *Took the Shuttle.*. Once taken, the gate holds nothing. **The hermit** now gives the way: *It is in the deepest room of Carrigbeg's Silence.* (`MAKER_REACHABLE` gains the Shuttle, as Session 796 said each trial would add its own). **The shape** is a placeholder: a pale spindle about a third of a unit long, with a thread end and a faint cold light so it can be found in the dark. The prop is owed to the look builder (H). The draft says *under the sigil*, but a generated gate has no sigil stone inside (only the seven legacy seeds of `SIGIL_PLACEMENTS` do), so the line stands as written over a room with none.
### Verified (headless Chromium)
`tests/shuttletrial` (new), 10 of 10. The place is *Carrigbeg's Silence*, a dry home-island sigil cave gate, not the blade's (189762), and the same on a second call. Down it, the Shuttle lies on floor 2 on open floor, 99 cells' walk from the stair, where the farthest open cell is 101. Driven by the game's own loop: at 3.5 units the line is said once, and on the other side of it nothing more is said. At 0.8 units the prompt reads *Press 'E' to take up the shuttle*. At Intelligence 20, E gives the failing line, nothing is taken and the try is recorded (n 1). At 35, the taking line and the log line naming the gate; *The Shuttle* is in the bag, unique; the mesh is gone and so is the prompt. A second visit lays nothing, and the blade's gate has none. The hermit's *The Weaver's?* gives the way to it, and *Gone from where it lay* once it is taken. No page errors. `makershermit` was changed for the hermit's new entry (it now offers the Beasts', the Hearth's, the Weaver's and the seventh). Found while running the neighbours, a correction to Session 782: the game's clock runs in fractional minutes, so three weeks added up in pieces could come to 10,079.999 minutes and count one week fewer (`shuttle` failed on one boot and passed on another). `tickShuttle` now counts a week within a millionth of a minute and never lets the remainder go below zero; `shuttle` reads the remainder to that tolerance. Neighbours green: `shuttle` (with `shuttleclaim`, `shuttletrial`), `makershermit`, `makertools`, `journal`, `bladekey`, `lairmaster`.
### Needs eyes
Whether the farthest room of a 100-cell floor-2 walk, behind the gate's whole roster, is the right weight for a tool whose real gate is Intelligence 35. The placeholder's look in a real dungeon's dark: the faint light is what makes it findable. The draft's *under the sigil* over a room with no sigil stone. And the place rule above, the seed's gate for *the gate nearest the last unread sigil*, is a reading that Michael can overturn.

## v80 — Session 801 — The Drowned Bell's trial: a wreck on a rock the sea owns twice a day (the approved draft, second run §2)
Session 778 built the bell's virtue and cost, and Sessions 788 and 794 its claimant and its once-only lines. Its trial was owed, and is built here in the draft's words. **Where.** The bell hangs from the last beam of a wreck on a rock off a home-island port, picked from the seed (`artifactPlaces().drowned_bell`). The home island's ports are put in the order of `seededRng('artifact','drowned_bell')`. The first port with open water off it wins, and one of its points is drawn from the same stream (`bellSpot`): along 24 bearings, the first point 50 to 140 units out where the bare land mask (`seaBare`, which reads nothing loaded) is sea, with open sea 14 units around it. So the rock lies within sight of a quay, as the draft asks, and is the same from any boot. In this world it lies 100 units off *Carrigcarra*. **The tide.** The rule is the game's `isTideOut()`, low from 0 to 6 and 12 to 18, as the canon's *the sea owns them twice a day*. The world's sea does not rise and fall, so the wreck does. At high tide it sits 2.4 lower and only the mast stands out of the water; at low tide the ribs, the beam and the bell are out. It eases over half an hour either side of each turn, a cosmetic only (`bellLowness`). The wreck is built within 400 units and dropped when you leave (`tickBellWreck`, once a second from the loop). **The trial.** The first time you come within forty units, the draft's line for the tide is said once (the character's `stats.bellSeen`): *A mast stands up out of the sea…* at high tide, *The sea has drawn back off a rock…* at low. From then the Journal's *Things not yet yours* carries the draft's line, *The Drowned Bell — in the wreck on the rock off ${coast}. At low tide.*, because the bell has no attribute and so no failed check to put it there. At high tide there is no prompt, and E within 3.2 of the mast says *The sea has it now. It gives it back twice a day.* At low tide, within 2.6 of the bell or 3.2 of the mast, *Press 'E' to take the bell*. E takes it (`takeArtifact`; the bell has no check), with the draft's *The bell comes off its beam green to the lip…*, and the log reads *Took the Drowned Bell from the wreck off ${coast}.* The wreck stays. At low tide the prompt is then *Press 'E' to look at the wreck*, and E says *An empty beam…*. At high tide E finds nothing there. **The hermit** gives the way (`MAKER_REACHABLE` gains the bell). **The rumour** (*There's a wreck on the rock off ${coast} that only shows at the ebb…*) is told while the bell hangs there, at Gatelands sites within a cell of the wreck that are ports or within 500 units of it, as the draft's *coastal Gatelands sites within a province*. **The shape** is a placeholder: a grey rock from the sea floor, the game's broken hull (`wreckGeo`) on it, a mast, a beam and a small green bronze bell. None of it is solid, so you swim to it. The prop is owed to the look builder (H).

## v80 — Session 803 — One name per bridge (the producer's filing: two *Border Road Bridge*s)
The producer filed this on 13 Oct. `poinames` (Session 756: no two named places in the world share a name) failed twice on PR #268's CI with two places called *Border Road Bridge*, and passed on main that morning on the same code. Michael's A on the unblock sent the clash here. A bridge is a site made when its cell loads (`buildBridges`, `82-world-structures.js`), named for its river, or for the road when the river has no name. Every road out of a province to the next is *the Border Road*, and a river crosses many roads. So the clash shows whenever two such cells happen to be loaded, which is why CI saw it and the local run did not. Walking into ten cells with border roads built 43 bridges: five *Border Road Bridge*s, two *Stanwater Bridge*s in one cell, two *Tradou Road Bridge*s in another, and more. Session 756's pass ranks the places a cell is made with; bridges come later and were never in it. Now a bridge whose name is already held by a place anywhere in the world gives way to the nearest settlement's name, *X Bridge*, and if that is held too, to both, *X Stanwater Bridge* (`bridgeName`). The nearest settlement is read from the cell's and its eight neighbours' data, not from what is loaded. No new words: the forms are the ones the world already uses. Which of two bridges keeps the plain name still depends on which loaded first. That is cosmetic (nothing is keyed by a bridge's name, and a site's id is its cell and index). The edit is in the look builder's file, at the one line that names the bridge; the bridge's build is untouched.
### Verified (headless Chromium)
`tests/bridgenames` (new), 3 of 3. Walking into ten cells with border roads builds 41 bridges, each named *… Bridge*: *Houfeirey Bridge*, *Saint-Vert Bridge*, *Nordou Bridge* and others where the plain names were taken. No two named places in those cells share a name, and one *Border Road Bridge* is left. On the previous commit's code (`--src`) the same walk builds 43 bridges, and the names check fails with *Stanwater Bridge*, *La Sauvage Bridge*, *Tradou Road Bridge*, *Border Road Bridge*, *Donaen Road Bridge* and more doubled. `poinames` and `bridges` green. No page errors.

## v80 — Session 807 — `dunwarm` counted the lights between frames; it counts them as drawn now (CI health, tests only)
The first item of the run's list is CI health: the suites Session 804 names FLAKY, worst first. This container cannot read CI's log store directly, so the 27 red jobs of 11 to 13 Oct were read through the GitHub tools. Each failed one suite. The screenshot timeouts in `pauseleaf`, `settingsheet` and `dmgnums` were 9 of them, and `dunwarm` 4. `poinames` was 3, all *Border Road Bridge* and all before Session 803 fixed the bridges. `shuttle` was 1, the 10,079.999-minute week that Session 797 fixed. Ten other suites failed once each. `saveui` and `hourhitch` did not fail in that window. The list is in backlog K. `dunwarm` failed the same way all four times: after a kill in the haunted gate the scene held 21 point lights against the pool's 20, and nothing had compiled. The pool (`_sweepScenePool`, `68-dungeon-misc.js`) runs each frame just before the render. It takes any new light out of the scene into a virtual source and maps the nearest onto the 20 it keeps. So a light added between two frames, by a timer or a foe's effect, sits in the scene until the next frame's sweep, and a count read then finds 21. The test read the count in its own `page.evaluate` after waiting four frames, which is between frames. The renderer never saw 21, and the compile count of zero in all four failures says the same. The game is right and the test read the wrong moment. The suite now wraps `REN.render` and records the light count of every draw of the dungeon's scene. Its check is that every frame drawn after the kill holds the pool's 20 (and the count before the kill is read the same way). A third check does what CI caught: it adds a light between frames, reads the scene at 21, and then sees the next frames drawn at 20 with nothing compiled. No game code changed, so the build tag stands.
### Verified (headless Chromium)
`dunwarm` 4 of 4. It looked at 70 foes of 13 kinds in three gates, with nothing compiled on sight. In each gate the kill's frames were drawn at 20 lights (minimum and maximum), with nothing compiled. A light added between frames: the scene held 21, the next three frames were drawn at 20, 20, 20, and nothing compiled. Of the two suites Session 804 named, `poinames` and `pauseleaf` were green here once each.
### Needs eyes
Nothing in play. Over the next day of CI, `dunwarm` should drop off the FLAKY list.

## v80 — Session 811 — `lairdoor` loads its door's cell again before it walks in (CI health, tests only)
One more of the suites that failed once on CI in 11 to 13 Oct. `lairdoor` crashed on CI with *Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'x')*, reading the door's place after it came out of the cavern. The suite measures the lairs round the start by loading their cells, up to four away, with `WORLD.loadCell`. It then walks into the first lair's cavern by its portal. The world's own cell tick (`tickCells`, every 0.75 s of real time) drops any cell more than one from the player, with its doors, portals and `dungeonWorldPos`. When a tick fell between those two steps, the portal was gone: nobody went in, the suite's wait for the cavern ran out, and the read of the door's place threw. A first guess, that the cell had not reloaded after the cavern, was wrong. A probe showed that in the failing run the player had never left the world. The suite now loads the door's cell again just before it looks for the portal, and if the door is missing it returns that instead of throwing, so the next check names the fault. No game code changed, so the build tag stands.

## v80 — Session 812 — `shiplog` reads the dial in a clear sky (CI health, tests only)

On CI, `shiplog` read two values exactly 1% short: 5.94 where it wanted 6.0 at hull 45, and 17.58 (*17.6 kn*) where it wanted the cutter's 17.76. ## v80 — Session 813 — `fortwalk` judges the walk on the distance, not on its rounding (CI health, tests only)
One more of the suites that failed once on CI in 11 to 13 Oct. *Every fort is walked on foot … to the keep door* failed on CI with every fort reached in 7.4 s and none stuck. The first, Cnocowen Keep, read *best 1.6* and the rest 1.59. The walk stops when the distance to the door is under 1.6, but the suite stored that distance rounded to two places and then checked the rounded value against `< 1.6`. A door reached at 1.5996 is stored as 1.6 and fails. In node, `1.5996 < 1.6` is true and `+(1.5996).toFixed(2) < 1.6` is false. How close a walk ends to the line depends on the step the runner's frames give it, so the result was chance. The walk now records `reached` from the raw distance, and the check reads that. The rounded `best` stays in the detail for reading. No game code changed, so the build tag stands.
### Verified (headless Chromium)
`fortwalk` green: every fort walked to its keep door in 7.4 s, its prompt, in and out.
### Needs eyes
Nothing in play. Of the list in backlog K, `lod` is left: its distant copy's shadow changed no pixels on one CI run (13 Oct).

## v80 — Session 814 — `lod`'s shadow control reads the mean difference when no pixel crosses the line (CI health, tests only)
The last of the suites that failed once on CI in 11 to 13 Oct. `lod` photographs one person's shadow four ways: cast by the full mesh, by the distant copy, by another person's distant copy (the control) and not at all. It counts the pixels that change by more than 24. The check wants the shadow to be there (2,090 pixels on CI), the copy to change under a tenth of that (0), and the control to change more than the copy, to show the comparison could see a wrong shadow. On CI the control changed 0 pixels too, so *more than the copy* failed. Its mean difference was still twice the copy's: 0.028 against 0.014, where the same frame drawn twice gives 0. Session 172 met this before: another person's shadow can sit close enough to the subject's that no pixel clears the threshold, and it picked the four most unlike people to make that rarer. When neither changes a pixel past the threshold, the control is now read on the mean difference, which must still be greater than the copy's. The main claim (under a tenth of the shadow's own pixels) is unchanged, and a control that cannot tell the shadows apart on either measure still fails. No game code changed, so the build tag stands.
### Verified (headless Chromium)
`lod` green. Here the control changed 706 pixels, the copy 0 (mean 0.01) and the shadow 1,670. Put through the old and new checks, CI's numbers fail the old and pass the new. A control with the copy's own mean difference still fails the new.

## v80 — Session 804 — A failed suite gets one more try before CI goes red; the logs stop conflicting (tests and settings only)
Michael asked why the board always holds four to six items blocked for days. The cause is mostly CI. Since 10 Oct there were 87 CI runs: 40 were cancelled by a newer push, 36 passed and 9 failed, and 13 more needed a re-run to pass. Almost every red was one of a handful of suites failing on code that passes elsewhere: `poinames`, `pauseleaf`, `saveui`, `hourhitch`, `dunwarm`, `shuttle`. With about 400 suites in 12 shards, one such failure turns the whole commit red. The producer re-runs once (another 50 minutes), and a second red becomes a "merge anyway?" card for Michael. On top of that, every branch appends to `docs/devlog.md` and `docs/decisions.md`, so each merge into main left the other open PRs conflicting there, and each conflict cost another CI run and another chance of a flake. PRs #261 and #262 hit this twice in a day.

**The retry** (`tests/run.mjs`):
- A suite that fails is run once more, on its own, before the shard is called red.
- If the retry passes, the shard stays green. The suite is named FLAKY in the summary, in `tests/out/flaky.txt` (ignored by git) and, on CI, as a warning annotation on the run, so it is still found and fixed.
- A real fault fails twice and the shard is red as before.
- The retry is skipped when it could push the shard past its budget: CI stops a job at 60 minutes, and the runner allows 50, less the time already spent, for a retry of the suite's usual length.
- `--no-retry` turns it off for a local run.

**The logs:** `.gitattributes` merges `docs/devlog.md` and `docs/decisions.md` with git's `union` driver, so two branches that each appended an entry merge without a conflict. It works for `git merge`, which is how the builders and the producer bring a branch up to `main`. GitHub's own mergeability check does not read it.
### Verified
- Two throwaway suites, one failing on its first try and one failing every time, removed afterwards. The first was named FLAKY with exit 0 and the CI warning line; the second failed twice with exit 1. With `--no-retry` it failed once and exited 1. `deadtree` passed as before.
- A throwaway repository with the same `.gitattributes`: two branches each appended a devlog entry at the same place, and `git merge` kept both with no conflict.

No game code changed, so the build tag stands.
### Needs eyes
- Over the next day of CI, the share of red runs should fall from about a third to the real faults. The FLAKY warnings name the suites the systems builder should fix first; `poinames` is a real bug (a name depends on which towns had loaded).
- Session numbers: Session 770 is used twice, once by the systems builder's woken householder and once by Michael's people-from-a-genome session. Both stand as history.

## v80 — Session 804 — The human builder: a tool page, saved genomes, and hair that lies on the head (B1, prototype only)
The look builder's first carry-over item while the foundation's renderer waits: B1 of `docs/design/character-builder.md`, Session 770's `people.js` made into the tool page, with genome save and load, and the women's long hair and braids fixed. Session 770 left the hair as its weakest part ("untidy at the temples"). A fresh render of its line-up showed why: every card was combed by one fixed direction and then fell free, so at the temples and the crown the cards crossed and stood off the head in planks, and the long hair was a tangle over a bald strip.

**The hair, rebuilt (`people.js`, `buildHair`).** Every strand now walks over the head's own surface at a small height of its own (its layer, 3 to 14 mm), found through a 2.5 cm grid of the morphed body's points and normals, and it goes where the style sends it. The styles:
- *short* and *loose*: from a centre parting, back over the crown and down the sides, never forward over the brow. Loose hair leaves the head at the occiput and falls as a curtain, spread by where its root sits and kept clear of the neck, the tunic and the fur mantle.
- *braid*, *braids*, *tail*, *bun*: every strand goes to a gathering point on the surface (the nape, behind each ear, the crown), routed back over the top rather than across the temple. The gathered part is built whole. A braid is three locks crossing in the classic figure (a sine across, twice the frequency in depth) along a line that falls under gravity, is pushed off the body by the clothes it wears, then smoothed, with a leather tie and a short brush. A tail is 260 cards in a widening bundle on the same line. A bun is one lock coiled two and a half turns, domed out from the head.
- The cards lie flat, their width along the strand crossed with the skin's normal under it, which is what makes the temples tidy.
- Roots grow from a wider region than Session 770's scalp: down to above the ears and to the nape, so a style that lifts the hair does not bare the sides. The hairline at the brow is 1.2 cm lower, and the cap under the cards is darker so it reads as hair.
- All of it comes from a stream seeded by the genome's seed, never `Math.random`, so one villager's hair is the same for everyone (the co-op rule).

**The saved genome** (`toSaved`, `fromSaved`): `{species, v, seed, people, sliders, race, palette, hair, dress, pose}`, with colours as hex and numbers to three places, about 730 bytes. `rollGenome(seed)` rolls a Markfolk genome from a seed, women's hair drawn from braid, two braids, bun, tail and loose, men's from short, tail and two braids. The four peoples' ranges are B3.

**The page** (`builder.html`, `builder.js`):
- a seed box and Roll, with a lock on every slider so the rest can be rerolled around it;
- 6 body and 17 face sliders, skin, hair and eye colours, the hair style, its length and the beard;
- every garment on or off with its colour, and the skirt;
- views: full, head, face, side and back, with drag to turn and the wheel to zoom;
- the genome as live JSON text, with *Save .json*, *Load .json*, *Apply text* and *Copy link* (`?g=` carries the genome in the URL).

`?sheet` puts every hair style on one genome side by side, for the pictures. The 1.8 m post stands beside the person.

`people.html`, the street and the gate pages still build: `markGenome` now draws a hair style, so their people's hair changed with this session.
### Verified (headless Chromium)
`node docs/prototypes/levelup/builder.check.mjs` (needs the pack from `mh_pack.py`): 60 checks, all pass.
- **Genomes:** five seeds roll, save, load back to the same genome byte for byte (713 to 741 bytes), and roll again identically. A loaded genome builds the same body and hair twice (a hash of every mesh's positions).
- **Each of the six styles,** with the mantle and without:

  - no strand point under the skin (0 of 20,000 to 124,000);

## v80 — Session 805 — The wardrobe's first pieces: the cloak, the hood, the apron, the brooch (B2, prototype only)
B2 of `character-builder.md` is the wardrobe kit. Its brief waits on Michael's marks for the second round's clothing sheets (OG-109 to OG-111 are still unreviewed), so this first slice takes only what the kept sheets already show:
- OG-048 and OG-059: the Gatelanders' hooded wool cloaks pinned at the throat with a round brooch, the farm woman's apron and the tradesman's long leather apron;
- OG-025: the Markmen's fur-lined cloaks on round iron clasps.

**The cloak** (`people.js`, `buildCloak`) is cloth hung from the shoulders, built after the pose on the posed body. The body is skinned on the CPU (three's `getVertexPosition`), so the cloak falls over the arms where they really are, not where the A-pose had them.
- **The drape:** 34 columns round the base of the neck each start on the shoulder line (the surface point furthest out and a little down from the neck at that angle). Each falls under gravity, using the drape the braids use. It is pushed clear of the body by what the body wears: 4 cm over a tunic, 9.5 cm over the fur mantle.
- **The sheet:** neighbouring columns are held to a spacing that may widen toward the hem by up to 1.5 times. Folds are rippled in, deepening toward the hem and fading at the front edges, and the grid becomes a double-sided sheet of 4,600 to 9,200 triangles.
- **The opening and the brooch:** the cloak opens at the throat, where a round brooch with a boss pins it (brass, or iron for the Markmen).
- **The collar:** a fur collar of six shells may be turned out round it (`cloakFur`). Otherwise the hood lies rolled behind the neck (`hood: 'down'`).
- **The hood up** (`hood: 'up'`) is a skinned garment, so it follows the head. The head's points are set out onto a smooth shell round the head and hair, which falls to the shoulders, with the face cut open in the shader.

**The apron** is the skirt shell's front with clean shader-cut edges, in wool or leather, with an optional bib off the tights' front.

**Saved and shown:** the genome saves all of it: `cloak`, `cloakFur`, `brooch` and `apron` as colours, and `hood`, `cloakLen`, `bib` and `apronLeather` as flags (770 to 800 bytes). The builder page gains the four garments, a hood selector, bib and leather boxes and a cloak-length slider, and `?dress=` sets garments for the pictures.

## v80 — Session 806 — The four peoples as ranges over one body (B3, first slice, prototype only)
B3 of `character-builder.md`: the four peoples as slider ranges over the one human body, so that a crowd is a people and a seed. `PEOPLES` in `people.js` takes the canon's peoples table (§2), the kept sheets (OG-048 and OG-059 for the Gatelanders, OG-025 for the Markmen, OG-044 for the Aurennais, OG-066 for the Old Blood) and Michael's 1 B (the heroic hybrid, about 1.80 m, with room for the tall Markmen and the short Old Blood).

**What a people sets:**
- **Stature in metres.** MakeHuman's height slider is not metres: the first line-up put a Markish man at 2.25 m. So a people gives a range of statures, and `heightFor` turns the stature into the slider by measuring the morphed body, crown to sole, in nine halvings.
  - Gatelanders: men 1.72 to 1.84 m, women 1.60 to 1.72 m.
  - Markmen: men 1.84 to 1.98 m, women 1.72 to 1.84 m.
  - Aurennais: men 1.74 to 1.86 m, women 1.62 to 1.74 m.
  - The Old Blood: men 1.56 to 1.66 m, women 1.46 to 1.56 m.
- **The body:** muscle and weight ranges (the Gatelanders wiry, the Markmen broad, the Aurennais lean, the Old Blood slight), and the mix of MakeHuman's three ethnic targets (the Aurennais mixed).
- **Colour:** palettes of skin, hair and eyes. The Gatelanders are fair to ruddy with red or dark hair; the Markmen pale, ash-blond and grey-eyed; the Aurennais olive through deep brown, dark-haired and brown-eyed; the Old Blood grey-pale, black-haired, with pale cold eyes.
- **Hair:** the weights of the hair styles, by sex.
- **Dress:**
  - Gatelanders: madder, moss, ochre, sea blue and undyed; hooded cloaks with a brass brooch for two in three, and aprons.
  - Markmen: the fur mantle and fur-collared cloaks on iron.
  - Aurennais: linen, blue and saffron.
  - The Old Blood: slate, oxblood, dusk violet and bone.

`peopleGenome` starts from Session 770's Markish roll (for the face and the pose) and lays the people over it. `rollGenome(seed, {people})` uses it, the builder page has a people selector beside Roll, and `?peoples` stands three of each in a line.

Not in this slice, all owing a skin texture or a new piece: the Old Blood's marks (pale raised lines under the skin, Michael's 2 B), the Gatelanders' freckles, Aurennais curls, head-wraps and sashes, and the named cast's genomes.

## v80 — Session 815 — One builder for people and creatures: one genome format (B5, prototype only)
The next creature-kit item in `character-builder.md` (B5): "the kit on the builder's page with the people (one tool, one genome format)". B1 to B3 each wait on a decision of Michael's (the hair, the wardrobe's method, the peoples' heights and palettes), and this item depends on none of them. Until now the two kits saved differently. A person's genome was already an envelope, `{species: 'human', v: 1, …}` (Session 804). A creature's was the bare `{plan, seed, sliders, tint, light}` the bestiary page printed, with no loader and no check on what it read.

**The format** (`creatures.js`, `toSaved`/`fromSaved`):
- A creature saves as `{species: 'creature', v: 1, plan, seed, sliders, tint, light}`, with numbers to three places; 174 to 185 bytes for the 23 plans.
- Loading rebuilds the genome from its plan and seed, then lays the saved values over it.
- A hand-edited genome is held to the sliders' ranges, a slider the kit does not know is dropped, and an unknown plan or a later version is refused with its reason.

**One loader** (`kit.js`, new): `readGenome(json)` gives `{species, G}` for either kind and refuses anything else; `saveGenome(species, G)` writes it back; `make(json)` builds it, fetching the people's pack (`mh_pack.py`) the first time a person is asked for and never for a creature. This is the file the game's loader becomes; it holds nothing of the page.

**One page** (`builder.html`, `builder.js`):
- The panel opens on a *kind*: a person, or any of the 23 body plans.
- **A creature's panel:** its source sheet, the seed and Roll, the gaits as buttons, the kit's six sliders with locks (Roll keeps a locked slider, as for a person), and the hue and lightness shift.
- **The views:** a creature has side, front, back and top. The camera is fitted to what each view sees, its length or its span, so a dragon from the front fills the frame. With the panel open, the view's centre moves into the open part of the screen.
- **On screen:** the creature walks on the spot in its gait. The 1.8 m post stands behind its tail. A swimmer gets the bestiary's water.
- **Genomes:** the genome text, *Save .json*, *Load .json*, *Apply text* and *Copy link* take either kind, and loading the other kind switches the page to it. `?plan=<plan>&gait=<g>` opens a creature, and `?g=` opens a genome of either kind.
- **No pack for creatures:** a page opened on a creature does not fetch the pack, so the creature half works without `mh_pack.py`.
- **The person's side:** nothing changes, except that the floor is 60 m across (it was 12) so the larger creatures stand on it.

## v80 — Session 822 — F1, the renderer: three.js 0.170 behind a switch
Card F1 of `docs/design/visual-foundation.md` §4, the first card of the new look (Michael's "Go with both of your recs", 12 Oct; Start given 13 Oct), run by the deep-work session under FREEZE #278. The game ran on three.js r128 from cdnjs. Every slice of the new look in `docs/prototypes/levelup/` runs on 0.170. F1 makes the same game run on 0.170 when switched on, with the old look whole and the default, so that F2 (scale) and F3 (the land) have one place where the version is chosen. No new art: the picture on 0.170 is meant to be today's.

**The bundle.** three.js stopped shipping a classic build after r160, and the game must stay classic scripts that open from a double-clicked folder (no `type=module`, no fetch over `file://`). `scripts/three_bundle.py` takes the npm package's `build/three.module.min.js` for 0.170.0 (the copy the prototypes already vendor, checked against a pinned SHA-256; the npm tarball if that copy is missing), puts the module body inside a function and turns its closing `export{a as B,…}` into `return{B:a,…}`. The result, `vendor/three.r170.min.js` (690,557 bytes, 415 names), sets `window.THREE`. No addons are bundled, because F1 needs none: the game merges its geometry itself. `--check` proves the committed copy is what the script makes, and CI's parse job now runs it. The bundle sits in `vendor/` beside `index.html`, so Pages and a downloaded folder find it, and so does the test harness, which writes its `index.local.html` beside `index.html`. That is why the bundle is not copied into `tests/vendor/` as the card suggested: one copy, found by all three. `parsecheck.py` scans only `js/`, so the bundle is outside it.

**The chooser.** One inline script sits in `index.html` just above the r128 tag and runs before any `js/` file. It reads `?look=new|old`, or else the setting `localStorage['og.renderer']`, and sets `window.OG_LOOK`.
- For the new look, it `document.write`s the 0.170 tag and then an opening `<template>`. The r128 tag that follows is parsed into the template's inert content and never runs.
- For the old look, the page is as it was: the same cdnjs tag, loaded the same way. A stray `</template>` after it is a parse error the browser ignores.

I chose this over the other ways for three reasons:
- **Every r128 tag written by script:** Chrome may block a cross-site script that `document.write` inserts on a slow connection. That would put the default look at risk.
- **Both loaded, one kept:** this breaks "one page, one three.js".
- **A module or a fetch:** neither works on `file://`.

`document.write` of a same-origin script runs in order on `file://`, on Pages and in the harness alike.

**The compat layer, `js/05-compat.js`** (a new file at a free number before 10, its tag added in load order; parsecheck counts 43 files). It is the only place that reads the version: `THREE_LEGACY` and `SKINNED`. On 0.170 it puts back what r128 did:
- **Colour management off and the output linear**, as r128's defaults were. 0.170 converts hex and vertex colours to linear and the output to sRGB by default. The renderer is wrapped, so `REN`, the creator's portrait and the yard's preview all get it.
- **The legacy light scale.** r128 multiplied every light's irradiance by π and let point lights fall off as `(1 − d/distance)^decay` with a default decay of 1. 0.170 is physical: 1/d², a decay of 2, and no π. `useLegacyLights` is gone since r165. Six exact replacements in `ShaderChunk.lights_pars_begin` restore the old scale: ambient, hemisphere, directional, point and spot colour ×π, and r128's distance falloff. `PointLight` and `SpotLight` default to decay 1. A replacement that no longer matches throws at load, so a later version cannot change the lighting without anyone noticing. So the game's 110 `PointLight` calls need no new numbers.
- **`skinning: true`.** r128 needs it on a skinned material and 0.170 rejects it with a warning. It is spread in as `...SKINNED` on the two skinned materials (`PEOPLE_MAT`, `WOLF_MAT`); clones keep it.

Checked and left alone:
- **No uses in the game:** `outputEncoding` and texture `.encoding`, `THREE.Math`, the old `Geometry`, `RGBFormat` and the removed helpers. The game's canvas textures have no colour space on either version.
- **The water's and the sea's `onBeforeCompile` hooks:** the chunks they replace (`begin_vertex`, `color_fragment`) are still there in 0.170.
- **The chimney smoke's `ShaderMaterial` fog includes:** also still there.
- **The shadow pass:** in 0.170 it still tests an object's layers against the eye's camera (`WebGLShadowMap`'s `renderObject`). CLAUDE.md's rule therefore holds in both looks, and so does the townsfolk's swap inside `REN.shadowMap.render`.

**The setting.** The settings sheet has a *Renderer* row (*As it was* / *three.js 0.170*) as its own small group under the mouse's two rows. It sits at the end so that the sheet's keyboard paths are unchanged. The choice is kept in this browser.
- **On the title screen**, the card's "the setting reloads the page" applies: the page reloads at once.
- **In play**, the choice waits for the next load, and the row says *takes hold when the game next loads: save, then reload*. Reloading under a player would lose an unsaved day. I took this narrower reading of the card, and it is listed below for Michael.

`setRenderer('new'|'old',{reload:true})` does the same from the console.

**The harness.** `boot({look:'new'})` boots `?look=new`, and `node tests/run.mjs --look=new` (OG_LOOK) does it for every suite. `g.logs` collects the console's errors and warnings from the first line. `people.test.mjs` unpacks `vendor/` with HEAD's build. `run.mjs`'s time table guesses looknew at 200 s and lookpair at 420 s.

### Verified (headless Chromium)

## v80 — Session 823 — The hood up, made again: a cowl you cannot see through (B2, prototype only)
Michael approved the wardrobe's method on #274 (A, 13 Oct), with one note: *take another look at the Hood though, it's semi-transparent.* Rendered from four sides, Session 805's hood had three faults:
- **The face hole was too big.** The hood was the head's own points set out onto a ball, with a face hole cut in the shader that ran back to the ears. From the front you looked past the face into the hood and saw the sides of the head, which is what read as see-through.
- **The ear showed.** The ear's folded points were pushed out with the rest and came through as a red lump at the side.
- **It stopped at the skull.** The ball ended at the back of the head, so the nape and the hair showed under it from behind. Session 806 also noted that the crown's hair drew as skin.

The hood is now a cowl built on its own (`buildHoodUp` in `people.js`):
- **The dome** is a grid of 56 columns by 64 rows. It covers the head, the ears and whatever hair is left under it, and its radii are measured from the body: its front comes forward until every point of the head outside the opening is inside it, 8 mm clear.
- **The drape** leaves the dome sooner behind than in front, so it falls down the nape instead of sitting on the neck as a ball. It joins the dome along a smooth curve, with no crease. Its hem lies on the body's own shoulders and upper back at each angle round the neck (smoothed), clear of the cloak, and higher over a fur mantle.
- **The face opening** is a soft oval from the hairline to under the chin, with a slot below it to the throat where the cloak's brooch is. It is open in front only, so the sides and back of the hood are whole.
- **The edge** has a rolled hem, 7.5 mm thick, that follows the opening.
- **The inside** is shaded at 0.42 (a new `inner` option on `clothMat`), so the inside of the hood looks like the shadowed inside of cloth.
- **The skinning** copies each point's weights from the nearest point of the body, so the head turns the hood with it.
- **The hair** is tucked in while the hood is up. The cards are not built and the scalp's shell shows at the hairline, so no strand comes through the cloth. The genome keeps its style for when the hood is down.

The new hood is 8,700 to 8,800 triangles with its hem, against Session 805's 3,000 or so; most of the extra triangles are the drape over the shoulders.

## v80 — Session 824 — The eyebrows, drawn and filled with hairs (B1, prototype only)
Michael approved the hair's method on #272 (A, 13 Oct), but added: *eyebrows look pretty fugly still*. Session 770's brows were a band of the skin's triangles, y 0.748 to 0.757 on the unmorphed face, 1.2 to 5.5 cm out from the middle, under three noise shells. That gave them four faults:
- the ends were square and cut along the triangles' edges;
- they were the same thickness from the head to the tail;
- they read as a fuzzy block rather than as hairs;
- they sat a little high over the eye.

A brow is now a shape drawn on the unmorphed face (`browShape`), set from the eye's own centre (the helper's eye group):
- **The head** starts at a third of the eye's distance from the middle. It is a little thinner than the body and rises into it.
- **The arch** is two-thirds of the way out. The lower edge follows the orbit's rim, 12.5 mm over the eye's centre, rising toward the arch and dropping a little to the tail.
- **The tail** thins to nothing, 1.6 times the eye's distance out.
- **Thickness** is 6 mm for a man and 4.5 mm for a woman. Women's brows arch more. Both can be set from a genome's `brow: {thick, arch}`; nothing writes that yet.

**The hairs** (`buildBrows`). The brow is filled with 700 to 800 hairs a face, fewer toward the tail. Each is 4 to 9 mm long and half a millimetre wide, in three segments that lift off the skin and lie back down. The comb follows how brows grow: up at the head, out and a little up along the body, out and down at the tail, and the upper hairs lie down over the lower. A root is placed on the unmorphed face and carried to the morphed one through the triangle it falls in, so the brow follows every face the sliders make. Hairs are skinned to the head bone.

**The colour.** Brows are drawn a little darker than the hair on the head, and darker still for fair hair. The skin under the brow is shaded up to 20% darker, so the hairs read as one brow rather than a scatter.

The old `brows` selection is removed from the pack's regions.

## v80 — Session 832 — The Church of the Weaver, in the new kit (card F6, prototype only)
Card F6's next item after the Mark's lots is Aurenne's temples. The canon (§1.3) gives Aurenne "domes on the churches", and its towns are under the Church of the Weaver's Priors. The concept art draws the churches as a domed hall behind an arcade with a slender tower beside it: OG-061, Aurenne's board, and OG-043's temple row. None existed in the new kit.

`pieces.js` has `aurenneChurch(o, r)`, at true size:
- **The hall:** a cube of lime-washed stone, 12 to 22 m a side and 0.8 m thick, on a podium with three steps down to the square. It has three tall arched windows on each side and on the back, each with a stone sill and an iron grille, and a dark room behind them. A band of the blue-and-white glazed tile runs under the cornice, and a parapet edges the flat roof.
- **The dome:** a drum with twelve arched lights, then the dome in blue glaze or limewash (`o.dome`). On its top is the Weaver's sign, a gilt shuttle on a rod. The first shuttle sat level across the rod and read as a cross from the square, so it now sits on the rod's tip and leans 22°.
- **The porch:** an arcade of five or seven round arches on turned columns, with an arch at each end. The great door stands behind it, 2.6 by 5.2 m: two leaves of cedar boards under a half-round head, framed in glazed tile.
- **The bell tower** (`o.tower`, 0 to 2): a square shaft of 3.6 m with slit windows, an open belfry with a gilt bell, and a small dome.
- **A cathedral** (`o.corners`) adds four small domes at the cube's corners and takes two towers.
- A cypress in a pot stands either side of the steps.

**Two changes to the shared kit.**
