## v80 — Session 828 — A town's people were always drawn the same; the test counted who had walked in (backlog I, CI health)
The merge of Session 817 found `townbarrels`' people hash unstable on the same code: Dunmore read two values, Portclare three, Cœur de Vie three over four runs, here and on CI. So the line was made a warning and the backlog asked the systems builder, after F1, to find what moves the draw. CLAUDE.md's S533 gotcha (an outcome that reads what had loaded) was the first suspect, through `dominantRegion` in `genSettlement`.

It was not the draw. A probe rebuilt each of the five towns in place (`disposeSettlement`, then `genSettlement`) under different loaded states, and Droichead came back with 11 people where it had 13. The two missing were villagers from `S.residents`. Residents are not built with the town. `tickSettlements` streams them in, two a tick, within 70 units of the player, and removes them past 95, and each one that arrives is pushed onto `S.npcs`. The hash read `S.npcs`, so it counted whoever had streamed in by the time the suite read the town, and that depends on how many ticks a slow or busy runner fitted into `g.settle`'s waits. Who a town draws was never in question. Restricting `REGIONS` to the town's own cell changed nothing either; the culture is read from the region at the pad's centre, well inside the cell, for all five.

The suite now hashes the people a town drew: its fixed townsfolk in order (the `S.npcs` that are not residents), then every resident in `S.residents`, whether streamed in or not. The line is a check again, with the five values read on main after F1 (`edda9f4`). Tests only; no game code changed.

### Verified (headless Chromium)
- **The probe, two runs side by side, the towns in opposite orders** (Dunmore first, or Droichead first): all five towns give the same drawn-people hash in both runs and again on a rebuild in place. Dunmore 715523239 (65 people), Carraig Mór 1906895553 (54), Cœur de Vie −459524478 (157), Portclare −1325179028 (37), Droichead −1790770419 (13). `S.npcs` held 23, 18, 34, 14 and 11 to 13 of them when the suite read it.
- **`tests/townbarrels`, two runs side by side:** 21 of 21 checks pass in each, the five people checks among them.
- `python3 scripts/parsecheck.py`: 43 files and their concatenation OK.
### Needs eyes
- Nothing in play: no game code changed. The new hashes include every resident, so a change that moves who lives in these towns will now fail the check, as the S753 and S817 sessions intended.
- Other suites read `S.npcs` too (`names`, `bornhere`, `twinsrebuild`, `townbio` and others). None of them compares a stored hash, but a suite that counts `S.npcs` reads the same moving list. None of them is on the FLAKY list today.

## v80 — Session 829 — `dunwarm`'s light between frames: 21 or more (CI health, tests only)
`dunwarm` went FLAKY on main's merge run of `c184194`, after Session 807's fix. The CI log cannot be read from a cloud session, so I ran the suite three times side by side here to load the machine as a runner is loaded. One of the three failed: *a light added between frames is counted (21) until the next sweep* read **22**. The frames drawn after it were 20, 20 and 20, and nothing compiled. The same run's haunted kill row also ended with 21 point lights in the scene between frames.

So Session 807's own finding struck twice at once. A foe's light, added by a timer or an effect between two frames, was already waiting for the sweep when the suite added its own light. The check counted exactly 21, assuming the scene stood at 20 at that instant. What matters, and what Session 807 wrote the check to prove, is that no frame is drawn with a light outside the pool. The check now takes 21 or more between frames and still requires every frame after to be drawn with 20 and nothing compiled.

### Verified (headless Chromium)
- **Before the fix, three runs side by side:** two pass. One fails on `{"between":22,"after":[20,20,20],"compiled":0}`.
- **After the fix, three runs side by side:** three pass. 70 foes of 13 kinds looked at, none compiling on sight. Each kill draws 20, 20 and 20 and compiles nothing. Between frames the scene holds 21, then draws `[20,20,20]`.
- `python3 scripts/parsecheck.py`: 43 files and their concatenation OK.
### Needs eyes
- Nothing in play: no game code changed.

## v80 — Session 830 — `lookpair` waits for the frame meter's reading (CI health, tests only)
**A correction first.** This run's two earlier entries were written as Sessions 827 and 828. PR #287 (`claude/art-round2-marks`, docs) already holds a Session 827, so before anything merged I renumbered them 828 and 829: the headings, the backlog's marks and the tests' comments. Their commits (`3137604`, `1b178ac`) keep the old numbers in their messages. Nothing was force-pushed.

`lookpair`, F1's side-by-side suite, went FLAKY on main's merge run of `edda9f4`. I ran two copies side by side here, and both failed the same check, *both looks measured their frame*, with `{"old":null,"new":null}`. The game's PERF meter reports once two frames 500 ms apart have been drawn. Each copy was drawing one frame every 5.5 to 7.8 s at that spot, so a fixed 9 s wait could end with no reading at all. The suite now waits at least 9 s, as before, and then until `PERF.last` is set, polling every 500 ms for up to 120 s. A flaky test waits for what it needs. ## v80 — Session 831 — `hourhitch` judges a frame against the run's own frames too (CI health, tests only)
`hourhitch` was on Session 804's list and went FLAKY on `0f94602` (auto/producer, 13 Oct). No fix had reached it since. I ran two copies side by side here, and one failed the frame-time check: worst 12,098 ms against a cap of 10,606. That frame came at the second jump to noon, with no shader compiled and no program added (the count stayed at 2 from the first dusk to the end). The cap was 8 s or twice noon's worst, and noon's worst is the slowest of 12 frames read once, at the start. That run read 5.3 s there, while its ordinary steps ran 6.4–8.6 s, so a cap of twice 5.3 s was tighter than the machine. The stall this suite hunts (the critic's s158) was 20–24 s with ordinary frames of about 4 s.

The cap is now the largest of 8 s, twice noon's worst, and twice the median of the judged steps' worst frames. On these runs that median is 7.2–7.4 s, so the cap is 14.4–14.8 s, and a 20–24 s stall would still fail it. The 4× noon clause and the two compile checks are unchanged: they are what catches a rebuild.

- **The floor:** dark slabs of 2.5 m, four across, with joints, low in roughness so they read wet. §2 says never cobbles.

- **The sigil:** the unread one, on the far wall at 3.4 m. It is a glowing ring of 2.4 m with an inner ring and twelve strokes, and two columns of script beside it.
- **The Shuttle:** 1.2 m out from the wall under the sigil, a little askew. A lathe of pale wood pointed at both ends and flattened, 0.32 m long, with its dark cavity, the pirn in it, and a thread end of 0.3 m lying from its eye across the slab ("a thread end in it that nothing will pull out").
- **`o.taken`:** the floor is bare.

The script is a canvas texture of amber strokes on black, drawn from its own stream (`gate-script`) so that making it once does not move the prop's own rolls. The kit's `put` now takes `uv: null` to keep a piece's own UVs: until then every piece's UVs were replaced by world-projected ones, and the script strips sampled their texture's black edge.

`trials.html?view=shuttle` looks from the door by torchlight: the script and the sigil glow, and the page carries more bloom. `&close` stands you over the Shuttle, and `&taken` takes it.

Added to **DECISION #298** as its sixth question:
- **A** (recommended): the trial's room is built as this one room at the end of the gate, so the Shuttle always lies under a sigil in the same light.
- **B:** the trial keeps the generator's deepest room, as Session 797 built it, and hangs the sigil on that room's end wall.

All six props are now prototyped: the blade's stone, the ring's cairn, the Waylamp, the bell's wreck, the cloak's den and the Shuttle's room. Each waits on #298 and on F2a.

## v80 — Session 852 — Card F9 begun: the Gatelands cottage as a room, inside its own shell (prototype only)
With the trials' props done, this session takes the next item in the look builder's order: places for F9 (rooms) as prototypes in the new kit. It starts with L9's *Homes as rooms*, from OG-115 (M7, the island cutaways: "a rural cottage of whitewashed stone and thatch with hearth, box bed and shelves") and OG-141 (P5: daylight through windows at four times, the hearth, candles and lanterns; "a Gatelands cottage lit by its hearth and lanterns"). Both sheets were opened and their catalogue rows read. Neither row's canon flags touches the Gatelands cottage: OG-115's flag is the Mark's "clans", and OG-141's is its cobbled dungeon. The FREEZE (#297) still holds, so this is a prototype only.

**The method: the room is built inside the very shell the street builds.** A new module, `docs/prototypes/levelup/rooms.js`, makes `gatelandsCottage(o, r)` from `pieces.js`'s `gatelandsBuilding` with the `GL_PLANS.cottage` plan. That is the house on the lanes: 9.6 by 5.4 m, walls 0.6 m thick, 2.7 m to the wall plate, thatch at 50°. One new flag, `plan.interior`, leaves out the dark box that otherwise fills every shell behind its windows (`pieces.js`, one line). The room's walls are the walls you saw from outside, at their thickness, with the same openings. The shell's black glass was made for a dark house, so inside the room it is swapped for a clear pane. At night you see the dresser through the window from the lane.

**The plan is a hearth-lobby house.** The cottage plan already put its ridge stack at x = −1.7, off-centre beside the half-door at −0.6. That is the Irish hearth-lobby layout, so the room follows it:
- **The lobby:** the front door opens into a lobby, screened from the fire by a jamb wall with a spy window.
- **The hearth wall:** it stands at the stack and runs up to the roof's underside. It carries a breast 0.55 m proud with an open hearth cut into it, sooted at the back, under an oak lintel, with a hearthstone before it. In the hearth is a turf fire of seven sods on embers, and an iron crane from the cheek carrying a pot. A door through the hearth wall leads to the room below (west).
- **The east partition:** deal boards, with a door at the front to the room above.
- **The kitchen:** a painted dresser on the back wall with three shelves of delft (one plate in three blue) and three crocks. A box bed of deal stands against the east partition, 0.9 by 2.0 m, with its red curtain, a straw tick and a blanket. A table stands under the front window, with a candle on it and two stools, and a súgán chair sits at the fire. The floor is flagstones in courses of 0.55 to 0.9 m.
- **The end rooms:** each has a bed and a chest, beaten earth underfoot, and a small grate in the east gable.
- **The roof:** three oak couples with their collars, and two purlins a side, under the thatch. The lantern hangs from the kitchen's collar.

`rooms.html` lights it at four hours, with the cottage's front facing south. `?view=kitchen|table|dresser|outside` and `&hour=morning|noon|golden|night` pick the view and the hour. The fire's light is always lit, the lantern from the golden hour, and the candle's flame burns on the table.

**Fixed on the way:**
- **The couples** came through the thatch, because each slope's rafter was tilted the wrong way.
- **The fire** sat inside a solid soot block. It now sits in a real recess in the breast.
- **The stools** stood in the way from the door round the jamb wall, and the table moved east.
- **A chest** stood inside the east room's bed.
- **The rafters' feet** reached 0.11 m into the back wall.

**What the light check found:** the first check asked for the noon sun on the floor and failed, and it was right to fail. At 52° the thatch's eave and the 0.6 m wall keep the high sun on the deep sill, as in a real cottage. The page's first morning sun, 62° off the wall's face, was stopped by the reveal. The check now asks for the south-eastern morning sun.

Asked as **DECISION #303**: *Rooms in the new kit: inside the street's own shell, and the cottage's plan* (two questions; recommended A and A).

## v80 — Session 857 — Card F8 begun: a Markish silver mine, built to the person (prototype only)
The FREEZE (#297, F2a) is still open, so this run works in the prototypes only. Card F9's rooms wait on DECISION #303, and the trials' props on #298. This session therefore takes the next item in the look builder's order that waits on nothing: L10's *Places that are not gates* (card F8), from OG-121 (N3: "mines and quarries: timber galleries and walkways over a shaft, ore and gems, cave-ins, a working site held by hostiles"). I opened the sheet and read its catalogue row. Its canon flags are the crypts' dead, Aurenne's "Roman" ruins and the Mark's Gothic castle, and none of them touches a mine. The Mark is the island for it: the canon's Mark sells "iron and silver from the ranges", and OG-121's Mark panel has "mountain mines". Who holds the working is the systems builder's.

A new module, `docs/prototypes/levelup/places.js`, makes `markMine(o, r)`. It is built to the person, one unit a metre:
- **The adit:** a level 18 m into the hill, 3 by 3 m in the rock. Timber sets every 1.5 m hold it, each two posts and a cap with lagging boards over the cap. The way between the posts is 2.07 m and the cap is 2.3 m up. A tramway of 0.6 m gauge runs on sleepers from the mouth to a stop-block on the landing, and the cart stands there half full of ore.
- **The stope:** the worked-out chamber the ore came out of. It is 12 m across and 16 m long, and 24 m high: 8 m over the adit's floor and 16 m below it, down to a sump of standing water.
- **The landing:** a timber deck across the chamber's near end, on joists let into the rock and posts down to the sump. A windlass stands on two sills out over the shaft, with its drum, crank, rope and kibble. A ladder goes down the east wall from a gap in the rail.
- **The gallery:** a walkway 1.4 m wide along the west wall, on beams let into the rock with a strut under each. Its rail runs along the open side.
- **The working face:** at the far end, on a ledge of rock left standing, the face is cut square and wet. A vein of silver-lead ore crosses it in shards set into the face's own surface, dipping a little. There are pick marks along it, broken ore and spoil at its foot, a pick against it, a basket, and a lamp on a peg.
- **The light:** nine lamps, the only light: three on the adit's sets, two on the landing's posts, two on the gallery, one at the face, and one let down in the kibble. A grey day comes in at the mouth.
- **`o.worked: false`:** the face is long worked out. The heap and the fresh pick marks are gone.

All the rock of a place moves by one noise field keyed by the place, so the adit's walls and the chamber's mouth, cut on the same half-metre cells, meet at the same points. The face has its own finer field, and the vein's shards are placed on that surface. The rock is a box seen from inside, smooth-shaded across its cells.

`places.html` has five views: `?view=mine` (default) from the adit's last set out over the landing to the lit face; `gallery` halfway along the gallery with the drop beside you; `face` at arm's length from the vein; `adit` from the mouth; and `shaft`. Add `&old` for the face worked out, and `&cam` for any camera.

**Fixed on the way, each found by the check or the pictures:**
- **The adit's corner:** the walk cut across it, so it now leaves the adit straight before turning for the gallery.
- **The planks** had 2 cm gaps that a ray fell through to the sump. They are laid edge to edge now.
- **The ledge's edge** is rough, so it pulled back from the gallery's last plank. The gallery's deck now runs half a metre onto the ledge.
- **The landing's posts** came 1.7 m up through the deck.
- **The vein** was first a smooth metal ribbon, then a row of pale stones the size of fists. It is now small dark shards in the rock.
- **The face** was a flat pasted rectangle until it was given its own rough surface.
- **The first frames were black:** the lamps were at a candle's strength for 0.170's units.

Asked as **DECISION #305**: *Places that are not gates: a Markish mine's measure, its light, and what comes next*. It has three questions: the levels' width (A as built, 2.07 m), what lights a mine (A, its miners' lamps while it is worked, and dark otherwise), and the next places (A: the Gatelands' round cairn, a limestone cave with a lake under falls, a smugglers' lair).

## v80 — Session 858 — Card F11 begun: the Gatelands sloop, clinker-built, at the game's own size (prototype only)
The FREEZE (#297) still holds. Session 857 left the places that are not gates waiting on #305, so this session takes the next item in the look builder's order that waits on nothing: L6's *hull line per island* (card F11), from OG-004 (J1: "Gatelands: clinker hulls, green sails with the harp, square rig"). I opened the sheet and read its row. Its canon flags are cannons on ordinary hulls, Aurenne's "crown jewel" and the invented heraldry (the lion and the wolf); the row's note says "the harp and the sun-star fill a gap". The game keeps its five classes, each dressed by its island (Michael's 3 A). The Mark's cutter and Aurenne's caravel already have hulls of their own in the game (Session 665), so the slice is the sloop, the Gatelands' own and the player's first.

A new module, `docs/prototypes/levelup/ships.js`, makes `gatelandsSloop(o, r)` at the game's sloop's numbers (`85-world-sea.js`): 13 m by 4.4 m moulded, draft 1.05, the deck 1.0 m over the sea (`DECK_Y`).
- **The lines:** the half-breadth falls to nothing at the stem and the sternpost, finer forward than aft. The keel's depth eases toward the ends. The sheer rises 0.75 m to the bow and 0.5 m to the stern. Each section has a round bilge and a little flare at the top. Toward the ends the low points draw in along the hull, so the keel is shorter than the sheer and the stem and sternpost rake out from it.
- **The strakes:** ten a side, each a real plank 3.5 cm thick, tilted so that its lower edge stands 2.5 to 3.3 cm outside the strake below and its upper edge tucks under the next. That is the clinker lap, and it reads as a stepped shadow down her side. She is tarred to the waterline and oiled oak above. The sheer strake is green under a cream wale. The strakes carry their own UVs, so the grain runs along the hull.
- **The deck:** fore-and-aft planks at 1.0 m, cut to the hull's half-breadth at that height, with a covering board along each side out to the planking. Amidships aft of the mast is a hatch with a 0.3 m coaming, and by the mast a coil of rope and a bucket.
- **The rail:** stanchions every 0.9 m with a cap rail 1.0 m over the deck, higher where the sheer rises (scale-numbers-build.md's "waist height").
- **The rig:** one mast, its yard at 9 m over the deck. The square sail is bellied forward and its foot is 2.2 m over the deck, so you walk under it. It is green with the harp, drawn on a canvas side on: the soundbox, the curved neck, the bowed forepillar and the strings. There are three shrouds a side, a forestay and a backstay, braces from the yardarms and sheets from the clews.
- **The helm:** the rudder hangs on the raked sternpost and its tiller comes inboard.
- **`o.harp: false`:** the sail is plain.

`ships.html` has four views: `?view=quarter` (default) from off her starboard bow; `side` broadside; `deck` from the tiller forward; and `lap`, close on the strakes at the waterline. Add `&noharp` for the plain sail.

**Fixed on the way, each found by the check or the pictures:**
- **Unseen planking:** the strakes were wound inward, so their outer faces would not have drawn. This one was caught by reading the winding before the first frame, not by the check.
- **Barrel staves:** the wood's grain ran up her side, because the world-projected UVs followed the normal. The strakes now carry UVs along the hull.
- **Open ends:** the half-breadth never reached zero at the stem and sternpost, so both ends were open, 0.36 to 0.42 m wide. The leak check's rays first got out there, once its reach was long enough to travel her length.
- **Too wide:** the flare made her 4.58 m wide. It is now 4.4 m.
- **Gaps in the deck:** the deck planks had 8 mm gaps a ray fell through, and nothing closed the deck to the hull at its edge.
- **A tub from the side:** her ends were vertical and her sheer flat, until she was given the rake and more sheer.

Asked as **DECISION #306**, with three questions:
- **The rig:** A, the board's square sail, so one rig names each island.
- **The harp:** A, keep it as the Gatelands' mark; B, plain; C, ask the quest writer first.
- **The helm:** A, a tiller on the small hulls and the wheel from the cog up.

## v80 — Session 839 — The cloak hangs in to the legs and falls in folds, and nothing comes through it (B2, prototype only; the bodies builder's first session)
Michael's A on #274 (13 Oct) kept the wardrobe's method, *drapes hang, shells fit*, on one condition: *as long as this doesn't have the arms phasing through the clothing.* The proposal he approved promised the cloak "deeper folds and a hem that comes in to the legs". Session 805's cloak had neither. Its 34 columns fell from the shoulders and hung straight down from wherever the arms and hands pushed them. The back flared out behind the legs, and the folds were a 2.2 cm ripple you could not see. Session 826 tried twice to pull the hem in point by point and parked both tries (`auto/wip-cloak-hang`: a crease down the back, a tear at the lower right). Its note said the next try should pull each column as one curve and fold by moving whole columns. That is what this session does (`buildHang` in `people.js`).

This is the bodies builder's first run, under FREEZE #297 (F2a), so it touches only the prototypes. The builder's files on main were older than auto/backlog's, so the first commit carries Sessions 823, 824 and 826 (the hood, the brows, brows by people) over from auto/backlog byte for byte. The two branches will merge without a conflict.

What the cloak does now, in order, all round the neck's vertical axis:
- **The columns are put in order.** The shoulder line crossed itself at the spine: at the centre back, columns 26 to 30 swapped places from the shoulders down. It was hidden while every column stood at the same radius, and showed as the sheet turned inside out once they came in by different amounts. Each row is now untangled so its columns run round the body in order, at least a third of the mean spacing apart.
- **A map of what is under the cloak.** For every 2 cm of height and 4° of angle it holds the furthest point of the body and, when a skirt is worn, of the skirt's fitting shell plus its push. The first version read every point in the pack, including MakeHuman's helper shells. The wide skirt helper made every side column look as if it touched the body down to the hem.
- **The column comes in as one curve.** Below the last row where it lies on the body (the shoulder, the arm, the hand), it comes in 75% of the way to the widest thing below it, along a smooth step over 35 cm. It never comes in past anything lower down that would push it out again. How far each point comes in is worked out per column, then smoothed across the columns before anything moves. Without that, the columns over the spine's groove dropped in alone and creased the back.
- **No sharp lobes.** Where the hand pushes the cloth out, the cloth rises to it and falls from it no faster than 1 cm out for 3 cm along the column, and only below the shoulders. A first try also spread this across the columns. It lifted the whole upper back and buried the braids, so it was taken out.
- **The folds are whole columns.** They follow a wave about six columns long (5.5 to 6.5, from the seed) that wanders. Each fold is up to 3 to 5.5 cm deep, deeper on a longer cloak, and grows from nothing below the shoulders to its full depth at the hem. A fold's trough never comes in closer than the body allows, so on the arms it is shallow. The hem rises on a ridge and drops in a trough.
- **More columns:** 56 instead of 34, so a fold is six columns wide rather than four facets. The cloaks are 7,700 to 15,400 triangles, against 4,620 to 9,240 before.

**The tunic through the cloak, fixed on the way.** With the first map (the body alone), the Markman's tunic skirt came out through the back of his cloak at the hip. The skirt is cut from the skirt helper and pushed out from it, and the cloak was coming in to the body under it. The map now includes the skirt, and so does the new check.

That is 0 of 5,898 points for the woman, 0 of 1,690 for the short cloak and 0 of 6,324 for the Markman. Before the skirt was in the map, the Markman's back failed this by eye while the body-only count read 0. The skirt is now counted.
  - **The hang.** The Markman's long cloak comes in 13.0 cm at the hem from its widest. The short cloak comes in 2.6 cm. ## v80 — Session 840 — The beard under a cheek line: no card under the eye or by the nose (B3, prototype only)
Session 826's close-ups of one man of each people noted two strays under *Needs eyes*: a dark wedge under the Old Blood man's eye and a pale card by the Markman's nose. The face pictures show the cause. Session 770's beard was every face triangle under a flat line at y 0.705, on the unmorphed body. The eye's lower lid is at y 0.715, so the beard's top reached within a centimetre of it. Its dark base shell took a triangle of the lower lid, which was the wedge. Across the cheeks it ended in a hard, jagged edge that followed the triangles, so a full beard read as a slab pasted on up to the cheekbones (`builder-man-face.jpg` before this session). The pale card was a moustache card rooted on the nostril's wing.

The fix is in `people.js`:
- **A cheek line** (`beardLine`). The beard's top runs from the sideburn by the ear (y 0.712, 7 cm out from the middle) down to the corner of the mouth (y 0.675, 3.2 cm out), on a slight curve. Inside the eyes' width that puts it 2.5 cm under the lower lid. This is the line a real beard grows to, cheekbone to mouth.
- **The base under the hairs.** The dark base shell is its own region now (`beardBase`), 8 mm inside the cheek line. The top edge of the beard is made of the hairs' roots, not a cut in a solid shell. That is 1,518 of the beard's 2,078 triangles.
- **The moustache over the whole upper lip.** It runs up to the nose's base (y 0.684) in the middle and comes lower toward the nostril's wing (0.4 mm for each millimetre out, to 3.3 cm). With the beard's top lowered, the first try left the upper lip bare: the moustache's roots stopped at y 0.678, and its cards hang downward.

Bearded men only change in their beards. Nothing else draws from the seeded stream in a new order, so every genome builds the same body, hair and brows as before.
### Verified (headless Chromium)
- **`builder.check.mjs`: all passed**, with one new check: the beard's highest triangle within the eyes' width is 2.5 cm under the lower lid, the moustache reaches y 0.684, and the dark base lies inside the hairs. Session 770's flat top would measure 1.0 cm and fail it.
- **Pictures, shot again:** `builder-man-face.jpg`, `builder-woman-face.jpg` (unchanged, no beard) and the six brow close-ups. The wedge under the Old Blood man's eye and the card by the Markman's nose are gone, and the cheeks above the beard are clear.
### Needs eyes
- **The mouth.** In the full face, the lips show through a dark gap in the beard at the mouth. That is the old mouth cut (an ellipse round y 0.655), and this session did not change it.
- **One line for every face.** Every beard follows the same cheek line. A Markman's beard that runs higher, or a trimmed Aurennais beard, is a genome number away and not set by `PEOPLES` yet.
- **The forehead's pale smear** on the right of every face picture is the skin's shading under the builder's key light, not the beard. It was there before.

## v80 — Session 842 — The Crown's tabard, crimson and gold, belted over (B2, prototype only)
The last piece named in the wardrobe plan Michael approved on #274 ("then do capes, hoods and the Crown tabard"). The kept Gatelander sheets draw the Crown's guards in it: OG-048 has a crimson cape and tabard with gold embroidery, and OG-059 a red-and-gold tabard. The canon gives the colours, *Crown crimson-and-gold* (§1.5, the mixing rules: national signage). It does not give an emblem. The catalogue notes that the device drawn on the sheets (a gold sun-cross) is the image generator's and that the emblem is a decision, so this tabard carries none.

`buildTabard` in `people.js` hangs two panels on the posed body, front and back. They are joined over the shoulders, open at the sides, with a hole for the neck.
- **The outline.** For each of 21 columns, the furthest point forward and back, and the top, of everything within 1.5 cm of the column's line: the body, and also the tights' shell under a tunic (with the tunic's own push at each height) and the skirt's shell under a skirt. The first version read the skin alone, and the tunic came through the tabard in green patches.
- **The hang.** Each column falls straight below the furthest point above it, the chest or the belly. It is taken in at the belt and falls straight again to the hem. The step in and out at the belt is smoothed over 4 cm down the column, and the panel is smoothed across the columns, never in past what is under it. The first version crumpled at the belt and was lumpy over the chest.
- **The belt is worn over it.** In the belt's band the cloth lies 2.5 cm off the tights' shell, or 4.5 mm over anything worn if that is further out. That is over the tunic (1.9 cm off the shell there) and under the belt (3 cm), so the belt shows clean across the tabard, as a guard wears it.
- **The cut.** The tabard is 0.56 of the shoulders' half width each side of the middle (37 cm on the checked man, 27 cm on the woman). The hem is 25 to 45 cm under the belt, set by `tabardLen`, so it reaches the mid-thigh. The neck hole is 6.8 cm each side, dipping 7.5 cm in front and 3 cm behind.
- **The colour.** The cloth is wool in the tabard's colour, with a 3 cm gold border round the sides, the hem and the neck. It is done in vertex colours, so it is one mesh and one draw.

The dress takes `tabard` and `tabardTrim` (colours, in the builder's garment list) and `tabardLen`. No people rolls a tabard: it is a role's dress (the Crown's guards and officials), for the cast and the roles still owed in B3.

## v80 — Session 845 — Two coat patterns in the kit: a pied cow and the badger's face (backlog L3, prototype only)
Sessions 843 and 844 each left a coat they could not draw, because the kit had only bands and stripes running along the body. The badger had no face, and its black-and-white stripes are the one mark everyone knows it by. The cow was plain brown, after the stripes came out as wavy bands. `dressFlesh` in `creatures.js` gains two patterns, read off the flesh at every vertex like the others:
- **Patches** (`pattern: { kind: 'patches', size, cut, tone }`). Where a slow noise, one cycle per `size` metres of the body, crosses `cut`, the coat turns to the patch tone. A finer noise gives the edge a little raggedness. The cow takes white patches 0.32 m across, which is a pied cow.
- **A face mask** (`face: { from, to, stripe, ground, back }`). On the head and jaw (where those bones carry more than half a vertex's weight), the distance out from the head's middle line is measured in the head's own radii. Between `from` and `to` the face takes the stripe tone, and elsewhere the ground tone, from the nose back past the ears and above the jaw's lower edge. The badger takes black stripes from 0.28 to 0.78 of its head's radius over white: the white blaze down the middle, the black bands through the eyes, white cheeks.

Neither pattern draws from the seeded stream, so every other plan builds as it did.
### Verified (headless Chromium)
- **`creatures.check.mjs`: all 298 checks pass**, with two new ones read off the vertex colours:
  - **The cow is pied:** 41% of its hide is pale.
  - **The badger's face is white with its stripes:** 1.00% of its hide is white with the mask and 0.00% without it (its ears alone did not cross the line). 32% of the hide is black.
- Every plan still builds, with its weights summing to one and its feet on their targets.
- **Pictures:** `creatures-cow.jpg` and `creatures-badger.jpg` shot again, `creatures-badger-front.jpg` new, and the sheets `creatures-livestock.jpg` and `creatures-common.jpg` rebuilt.

## v80 — Session 879 — F2a begins: on the new look, people are drawn again (the deep-work session, card F2a)
The first session of card F2a (the scale pass, `docs/design/v2-scope.md` §3), under FREEZE #297. The card puts one fault first, found by the critic on 14 Oct (backlog I, s627): on `?look=new` no person was drawn. three.js 0.170 gives a `SkinnedMesh` a bounding sphere of its own, computed once from the posed vertices through the bones' world matrices, so the sphere already sits in world coordinates (centre 13553.7, 9.7, 25405.6, radius 0.68, for a townsperson standing at exactly that spot); the frustum test then applies the mesh's world matrix a second time and puts the sphere some 30 km off. Every skinned body (townsfolk, guards, the player's own third-person body, wolves) was culled; only what they held showed. r128 culled them by the geometry's sphere in local space, which `32-people.js` already pads by 1.35 for a raised arm or a stride.

`js/05-compat.js`, the one place the version is read, now gives 0.170 r128's behaviour: `SkinnedMesh.prototype.computeBoundingSphere` (and `computeBoundingBox`) copy the geometry's own. Nothing changes on the old look, where the patch never runs.

`looknew` asserted that the townsfolk's bones move, which they did while nobody could see them. It now also stands 4 m from the nearest townsperson, looks at it, and asserts the mesh is inside the camera's frustum and that the scene draws one call more with it shown than hidden.

The before half of F2a's picture pair is taken here, before anything is scaled: `tests/f2ashots.mjs <tag>` (not a suite) writes Dunmore's square at noon, from 9 m south of the middle looking north, and the inn's room from its door, to `docs/prototypes/f2a/<tag>-*.jpg`. `before-dunmore-noon.jpg` shows the trouble the card is about: the man by the well stands about as high as its roof's posts are tall, and the club fills a third of the screen from an eye at 0.92.
### Verified (headless Chromium)
- Before the fix, on 0.170 the nearest townsperson in Dunmore at noon, 4 m off and looked at: `Frustum.intersectsObject` false, its sphere's centre at (13553.7, 9.7, 25405.6). After: true, the centre 0.74 from the mesh's origin, radius 1.26.
- `looknew` 11/11, the new check among them: inside the frustum, 854 draw calls with the person shown against 853 hidden.
- `lookpair` 1/1: the two looks' pictures of Dunmore match (mean difference 6.1 of 255), both measured their frame, no page errors.
### Needs eyes
- On the new look, the townsfolk, the guards and your own body in third person should be back. Nothing else differs.

## v80 — Session 880 — F2a: SCALE, and people at their true heights (the deep-work session, card F2a)
The second session of card F2a. One unit is now one metre with people as the measure (`docs/design/visual-foundation.md` §1), in one table. `js/07-scale.js` is a new file, tag 07, between the renderer's version and the player. It holds `SCALE`, in metres:
- the peoples' statures, a man's and a woman's middle (Michael's A on #276): Gatelanders 1.78 and 1.66, Markmen 1.91 and 1.78, Aurennais 1.80 and 1.68, the Old Blood 1.61 and 1.51;
- the 1.8 m figure the ratios are measured against, and the eye, 1.65 standing and 1.1 crouched;
- doors, the big door, the town gate, the storey, stairs, furniture heights, room sizes and ceilings;
- the third-person camera and the swimmer's eye (below).

`personScale(g)` gives a body's root scale from its people and sex. The layout rules are kept: the file loads before everything that reads it, and parsecheck passes over all 44 files and their concatenation.

**People.** `buildPerson` (`32-people.js`) is the one place a body's size is set, and it now multiplies by `personScale(g)`. I measured the body on the skinned mesh in its idle pose: at genome height 1 and its old root scale, the top of the head stood at 1.233 over the feet, with the head bone at 1.001. The card's figure of 1.05 to 1.15 had been read off the head bone. So `SCALE.PERSON_MODEL` is 1.233, and a Gatelander man of height 1 now stands exactly 1.78, a Markman 1.91, an Aurennais 1.80 and one of the Old Blood 1.61. That is a growth of 1.444 times, not the 1.6 the brief guessed.

The same path carries the rest:
- townsfolk, guards, and every foe built on the people's body: bandits, cultists, skeletons, goblins at their .72 and kobolds, trolls and ogres at their kinds' sizes;
- the player's third-person body (`54-thirdperson.js`, which builds at height 1 with your people).

Creatures (wolves, bears, spiders, the kit's animals) keep their size in metres, as the card asks; none read plainly wrong at a glance, and the critic should look.

One rule of motion had to follow, and it is not a speed. A person breaks into the run past `PW.RUN.on` *root-scales a second*. That threshold moved with the body, so a bandit chasing at 1.63 m/s walked. It is now divided by the growth, so the pace at which anyone breaks into a run stays the same in metres a second (about 1.25 m/s), and the world's speeds are unchanged.

**The eye and the cameras.**
- `EYE_STAND` and `EYE_CROUCH` read `SCALE`: 1.65 and 1.1, from 0.92 and 0.60.
- The first-person viewmodel draws in its own scene and camera (`VM_SCENE`, `VM_CAM`), so its placement does not depend on the eye and nothing in it clips at the new height. It is unchanged.
- The near plane stays at 0.05.
- The third-person camera's distance, its range and its shoulder offset grew with the body: 2.75 (from 1.9), 1.3 to 4.6 (from 0.9 to 3.2) and 0.5 (from 0.34). Its caps indoors and in a gate's floors went to 2.2 and 2.45 (from 1.5 and 1.7). The wheel's choice is saved under a new key, `og_tp_m`, since the old value was at the old size.
- A swimmer's eye stays where the old eye put it over the water (`SCALE.EYE_SWIM`, .92 over the swim floor, 0.57 above the sea): at 1.65 over a floor 0.35 under the sea, you would have trodden water with your shoulders out. `cameraUnderwater` reads the current eye, which comes to the same test.
- In third person, a swimming body sinks so that the top of its head is a quarter metre over the sea. The water's depths, wading and the dive are F2b's.

**Aim.** The crosshair finds a skinned body by capsules along its bones (S596). The head bone sits at the jaw, at .81 of the height, so from an eye at 1.65 the crosshair on a woman's face (head bone 1.35) passed over her. An end bone (the head, a hand, a foot) now carries its capsule on past the joint by .15 of the body's height. `talkaim` was red on this, and is green again.

**Suites re-measured, not loosened** (each says so in a comment):
- `people`: a person stood as tall as before; now they stand at their people's stature (Aoife 1.66, Brendan 1.72, Cathal 1.80) and within 1.55 to 1.95.
- `goblins`: the kobold's scale was under .7; now under 1.01, and still under .75 of a bandit's.
- `goblinbody`: the inspector's goblin is read over its people's stature, .543.
- `foes`: unchanged. It went green again with the run threshold in metres a second.
- **Not re-measured, because it was right:** a person's breadth by people. The world gave each people a stature and a breadth through `bodyScale` (`PEOPLES`, a Markman 1.08 tall and 1.1 broad), and that stature now comes from `SCALE`. Counting it twice made Markmen 2.13 m, so `bodyScale` keeps only the breadth over the stature (a Markman 1.02 broad).
### Verified (headless Chromium)
These ran on the working tree with Session 881's doors as well, which change no person.

**The house builder** (`buildingGeoHi`, `buildingGeoLo` in `82-world-structures.js`, every style on all three islands) now reads `SCALE` and holds no free number for a door or a storey.

## v80 — Session 896 — F2a: rooms at true size (the deep-work session, card F2a)
The fourth session of card F2a, item 4: interiors rebuilt at true size, without the ×1.8 footprint and the ×0.62 furniture heights. Before, `buildInteriorFor` made every room its house's footprint × 1.8 (and at least 8 across), in units where a man stood 1.23. To a 1.78 m eye, a 5 m cottage became a room 15 m across with knee-high tables.

**How it is built now.** The furniture kit (`furnBuild`, `56-dungeon-build.js`, the man it was drawn for 1.28 tall) and every layout in `buildInteriorFor` were drawn in that old unit. Redrawing them all in metres is card F9's work (rooms dressed by nation). F2a keeps them and changes the scale the room is built at:
- the room's **true size** is chosen in metres;
- it is laid out in the old unit at that size ÷ `SCALE.ROOM_K` (1.444, the people's growth, 1.78 ÷ 1.233);
- the finished room is scaled up by `ROOM_K` whole (`scaleRoom`).

So a table, a doorway or a stair stands to a 1.78 m person exactly as it stood to the 1.23 m one, which read right, and the room is its true size. `scaleRoom` moves every object out from the room's corner and grows it by k. The people are the exception: they are built at their true heights already, so they only move. The lights reach k further. Every record the game keeps of a room is scaled with it, each record once:
- the solids and the footholds;
- the beds and the doors, with their solids and boxes;
- the people's boxes, the bed's and the stash's places, the barber's chair, the hatch, the strongbox and the tower's chest;
- the room's size.

The keeper is placed after the scale, so laying a sleeper uses the scaled bed.

**The sizes, in metres** (`visual-foundation.md` §1):
| Room | Size |
|---|---|
| Cottage | 4.6 to 6 by 4.5 to 6 |
| Shop | 7 to 9 wide, with the keeper's room behind its partition (3.8 m more deep) |
| Barber | 8 to 9 by 7 to 8.5 |
| Inn | a hall 10 to 12 by 11.7 to 13, the gallery's rooms over its north end |
| Church | a nave 8 to 10 wide, 14 to 18 long |
| Cellar | 6 to 8 by 5 to 7 |
| Ship's cabin | 7 by 8 |
| The Guest's chapel | 9 by 12 |

A room may still be larger inside than its house is outside, as games do: the inn's hall and the church's nave stand in houses of 5 to 7 m, which F6 will grow.

**Three kept their old rooms, scaled up by k:** the keep's hall (26 by 32 m), the guild halls (32 by 29 m, the dormitories behind the hall) and the tower. The tower is not scaled at all, because its stair climbs to the 30 m its outside shows. The ceilings are the old ones in the old unit, 2.9 to 3.2 m true.

**The layouts that no longer fit were redrawn.** Each now shares its places with the solids (`homeAt`, `innAt`, `armouryAt`, `barberAt`, `churchAt` in the kit), so a table's solid stands where its mesh does:
- **The cottage** (3.2 to 4.2 across in the kit's unit):
  - the bed in the north-west corner, which has a solid now;
  - the hearth on the east wall, sized to the room;
  - the table a little north of the middle, with a chair at each end;
  - the chest under shorter shelves on the north wall;
  - the strongbox by the west wall near the door;
  - a weaver's loom against the south wall, a farmer's sacks and a cooper's barrels in the south-east corner.
- **The inn:**
  - the bar under the gallery;
  - the hearth on the wall the stair does not climb (it shared the east wall with the stair in half the inns);
  - as many tables with benches as fit between them, clear of the door's way;
  - the gallery at least 4.15 deep in the kit's unit, so its rooms behind the corridor are built: an upper room is 3.4 across in the kit's unit (it was 4.5), two rooms in a hall of true size;
  - the cellar's hatch in the corner by the door.
- **The smithy:** the racks down the east wall from the counter's end, the tub clear of the counter, the grindstone by the door.
- **The armourer:** two or three stands by the shop's width.
- **The barber:**
  - the washstand on the chair's west;
  - the stool on its east, and the barber stands there;
  - the dyer's corner kept inside the east wall.
- **The keeper's room behind a shop's partition:** the bed down the east wall, a small table at its head, the strongbox against the west wall, and the way from the door to the shop clear.
- **The church:**
  - the pews sized to the nave either side of the aisle;
  - the columns between the pews and the walls (at ±4.1 they would have stood outside a nave of true size);
  - the pulpit at the dais's corner.
- **The cellar:** the barrels down the west wall, the crates in the north-east corner, the wine rack sized to the room.

**What a player does in them:**
- You arrive 1.75 m inside the door in a small room (it was 2.2, the middle of a 4.5 m cottage), still clear of the step that leads out.
- Only inns and guild halls have galleries now. A two-storey cottage or shop of true size has no room for the stair, so its ground floor is all of it.
- **A save made inside a room before F2a** holds a spot in the old, larger room. If that spot is off the floor or inside something now, the load stands you at the door (`goToInterior`); full migration is card F13.
**Finished in a second run the same day.** The work began on `auto/wip-fable-f2a-scale` as "Session 882"; `auto/backlog` had taken 882 to 895 meanwhile, so it is Session 896 here and in the code's comments (a correction to Session 881's entry, which says the interiors' half of the ratio suite comes with Session 882). The run merged `origin/main` (the backlog kept both edits) and the WIP into the card's branch, and fixed what was still red:
- **The arrival in a shallow shop.** A goods shop 7 m deep with no keeper's room put you 2.1 m in from the door, inside the counter's front (4.91 m from the back wall at true size). `intArrivalZ(house)` (`58-interiors-legacy.js`) is now the one place the arrival is worked out, for a fresh entry and for a save's spot that no longer fits: 1.75 to 2.2 in from the door as before, and at least .55 in front of a counter (`buildInteriorFor` keeps the counter's front edge, `house._counterFront`).
- **The tower's door.** The tower keeps its old size, so its entrance was still the old unit's leaf, 1.72 m with its head, shorter than the man going through it. The door alone is now built at `SCALE.ROOM_K`, 2.48 with its head, as in every other room.
- **The church's tall windows.** A nave of true size (14 to 18 m) held two round-headed windows a side from the old spacing (from 3, every 3); it now holds three, as the old longer nave did (from 2.5, every D/4 but at least 2.2).
- **Window frames.** In a cellar (a 2.6 m ceiling) the frame's head stood .04 above the ceiling; the window sits lower when the ceiling is under 1.95 in the kit's unit. In a cabin of true size (8 m) the last window's open shutters passed through the end wall; a window keeps 1.05 from it, and the posts' window list follows.

## v80 — Session 869 — Card F8's second place: the Gatelands' round cairn with its passage (prototype only)
Michael's 3 A on #305 named the next places that are not gates: the Gatelands' round cairn with its passage, then a limestone cave with a lake under falls, then a smugglers' lair. The FREEZE (#297) holds, so this is a prototype. I opened OG-121 again and read its row. The Gatelands' panel draws "round cairns", and the row's one flag that touches them is burial: §3.1 gives the dead to the gates, so a cairn is an older or a refused custom, and who lies in one is the quest writer's to settle. So the basins are built empty, and the carving on the stones is asked.

`places.js` has a new `gatelandsCairn(o, r)`, built to the person:
- **The mound:** a grassed dome 26 m across and 7 m high on a polar grid, with its foot 1 m up at the kerb's line. It is moved by one noise field keyed by the place (the mine's `field`). The turf is the Mark kit's moss sod made green, with its UVs taken from above, so the texture does not seam where the slope turns.
- **The kerb:** 38 rounded boulders laid on edge round the foot, with a dry-stone wall behind them up to the mound.
- **The facade and the door:** where the door is, the mound is held back by a dry-stone facade on a chord of the kerb, 8.4 m wide and 3.4 m high over the door, falling to the kerb at either end. The mound's grid is pulled onto the chord inside the facade's thickness, and only the door is cut from it. The door is 1.25 m wide under a lintel at 2.2 m. A long entrance stone, 3 by 1.2 m, lies 2.4 m before it, and the way in goes round its east end.
- **The passage:** 10.3 m long, the floor rising 0.8 m toward the chamber. Upright slabs line both sides, each a little out of true, with dark dry-stone packing behind them. Lintels 0.95 m deep cross it, each set 2.2 m over the floor at its inner edge.
- **The chamber:** cruciform. The middle is about 3.8 m across under a corbelled vault of eight courses of nine slabs, each course 0.36 m high and stepping in 0.2 m, with a capstone at 5.98 m. There are three recesses, east, west and back, each 1.5 m wide and 1.6 m deep under its own capstone at 2.3 m. Each recess holds a shallow oval basin of stone, empty.
- **`o.carved`** (default true): three spirals and a vertical groove pecked into the entrance stone's face, a triple spiral on the back recess's end stone, and four lozenges up one slab of the passage. `&plain` builds the cairn bare.
- **The light:** nothing burns inside. The view gives you the torch the worked-out mine has (Session 868).

`places.html?place=cairn` has five views: `view=cairn` (default) from the approach; `door`, at the entrance stone; `passage`, by torch up to the chamber; `chamber`, from its mouth to the back recess; and `vault`, looking up into the corbelling. `places-view.js` hands `place=cairn` to the new `places-cairn-view.js`, and the mine's views are unchanged.

**Fixed on the way, each found by the pictures or the check:**
- **The mound was wound inward:** it drew black and see-through, with the vault showing through it.
- **The mound's texture seamed** in zigzags where the world UVs changed axis on the slope.
- **A sliver of sky over the facade:** the first cut took away every triangle pulled onto the chord, including those above the facade's top. Only the door's are cut now.
- **The stones were cubes:** the kerb and the entrance stone are rounded boxes now, and the facade is rubble (the kit's cobble) rather than coursed blocks.
- **Light at the recesses' corners:** 4 of 1,200 rays got out at the east recess's outer corners, where the packing behind two walls did not meet. The packing now runs 0.7 m past each end in the chamber, but not into the passage, where the first try narrowed the way to 0.52 m.

Asked as **DECISION #309**: what is carved on its stones? A, spirals and lozenges (the islanders' own oldest marks, older than the gates' script; recommended); B, the Weavers' script, cut and unlit; C, bare.
### Verified (headless Chromium)
- **`places.check.mjs`: 19 of 19 pass**, with eight new for the cairn:
  - **The builds:** 3 keys, each the same twice. 43,884 triangles in 7 meshes, with 38 kerbstones, 7 m high.
  - **The passage:** at 20 stations it is 1.25 m clear between the slabs at the hip (to 1.95 m where a ray finds the packing between two slabs), and the lintels are 2.16 to 2.28 m over the floor.
  - **The walk:** 90 points every quarter metre from the approach, round the entrance stone, in at the door and up to the back recess's mouth. Every point has a floor on its line (0 to 0.023 m off), 2.14 m of headroom or more, and 0.63 m clear at the hip and the head.

- **Pictures, new:** `places-cairn-cairn.jpg`, `-door`, `-passage`, `-chamber` and `-vault`.
### Needs eyes
- **The mound reads green and smooth.** A real cairn shows stones through its turf where it has slumped. The sides near the kerb also stretch the turf texture, because it is projected from above.

OG-121's caverns have "stalactites, an underground lake under falls, strange flowers, hidden entrances", and its Gatelands panel has "limestone caves". OG-099's Mistveil Grottos are "a cave of blue pools and a bridge under waterfalls". Neither row flags anything a cave touches.

`places.js` has a new `gatelandsCave(o, r)`, built to the person on the mine's shared rock (one noise field keyed by the place, amplitude 0.4 m):
- **The passage:** 14 m from the mouth, 3 m wide and 3 m high in pale limestone, on a flat bed.
- **The chamber:** 22 m across, 26 m long and 11 m high. Its walls run 4 m below the floor, so no slit opens where the floor meets them, and the near wall is cut for the passage.
- **The floor:** one grid over the chamber, run 0.8 m under the walls. The shore is flat at 0 along the east side (4.2 m wide), across the near end (3.4 m) and at the far end east of the falls' pool, where the far shelf is. Elsewhere it falls in a smooth step over 3.2 m to the lake's bed, 3.4 m under the surface at 0.45 m below the shore. The dry cells carry a pale limestone skin.
- **The falls:** a stream comes in through a swallow hole in the roof at the far west corner and falls 11 m to the lake, drawn as three wavering ribbons a little apart, with a ring of foam where it lands. Over the hole a wet funnel rises 12 m to the sky. It is 3.2 m across at its foot, just under the roof and wider than the hole cut in it, and 2 m at its top, so nothing gets out between the roof and the shaft.
- **The dressing:** 46 stalactites up to 2.6 m long from the roof (their tips 8.2 m or more over the shore), 16 stalagmites and 7 lobes of flowstone on the shore kept 1.1 m off the walk and back from the water's edge.
- **The flowers** (`o.flowers`, default true): six clusters of pale blue flowers that glow, at the water's edge along the shore.

`places.html?place=cave` has four views: `lake` (default), from the passage's end across the lake to the falls; `shore`; `falls`, from the far shelf up the falls to the shaft; and `passage`. The light is the day down the shaft onto the pool, a cool glow off the white water, the flowers' own glow, and your torch.

- **The swallow hole was cut in the floor's side of the roof:** the roof's faces point up, and the first cut looked for faces pointing down.
- **The falls landed in 0.15 m of water:** the lake's depth measured its distance to the far shelf with the wrong sign, so the far west corner stayed a shallow shelf.

- **The shaft's spot was too wide:** it painted straight-edged shapes of the funnel's shadow on the far wall. It is narrowed to the pool.
- **The view from outside the mouth** showed the cave's back as a box, since it has no hillside round it. That view now stands just inside the mouth, as the mine's adit view does.

## v80 — Session 882 — The limestone cave rebuilt at three times the measure, with its dressing (card F8, prototype only)
*Renumbered:* this run's sessions were first committed as 878 to 881, but auto/bodies had already written its own Session 878 (the beard at the collar). They are 882 to 885 in the devlog, the backlog, decisions.md and the prototypes' comments. The commit messages and the first PR comments keep the old numbers.

Michael answered A on #313: the day comes down the shaft and the flowers glow. He added a note: "I don't think this cave is expansive enough. This feels pretty underwhelming to me. I hope this isn't the scale we're going for in all of our dungeon interiors, especially Old Gates." His F2b answer (3 m cells) says the same of the gates, "extremely massive and cavernous", and allows a cave or a mine "a more typical size". The cave of Session 872 was too small even for that. It was a box of 22 by 26 by 11 m with flat walls, so the swallow hole showed as a ring in a flat ceiling, and it held nothing but cones. The FREEZE (#297) holds, so this is the prototype again. OG-121 and OG-099 were reread: OG-099 is "a cave of blue pools and a bridge under waterfalls", and the first build left out both the pools and the bridge.

`gatelandsCave` in `places.js` is rewritten. The returned shape is the same, with `walkY`, `bridge`, `columns` and `pools` added:
- **The hall is lofted ring by ring** (a new `loft()`). It is 64 m long. It is 30 m across at its ends and 46 m in the middle (35 m at the floor). Its crown is 16 m over the shore at the ends and 26 m in the middle, and both ends close in rounded domes. The rock is moved by noise at three sizes (4 m, 1.2 m and the place's own 0.35 m) and by nine alcoves and buttresses high on the side walls. The noise fades to a tenth near the floor, so the walls meet the floor cleanly and stay off the walk.
- **The cuts are by test, not by hand.** The hall drops its faces that lie inside the passage's tube or under the shaft. The tube drops its faces that lie inside the hall. Each cut has a margin of 0.4 to 0.5 m, so the two shells overlap and no slit opens where they meet.
- **The way in** is a passage of 22 m that winds 2.5 m either side. It is 4.4 m wide and 3.6 m high, and it comes out on a **ledge 4.5 m up** across the hall's near end, a balcony over the lake. A ramp of rock runs down the east wall to the shore at 1 in 4.4.
- **The shore** is a band 11 m wide down the east side. It steps down to the lake in **three rimstone terraces** of 0.25 m and 1.4 m, their edges wavy, with **30 blue pools** in low lumpy dams on them (OG-099). The lake's bed is 4.2 m under the surface.
- **A natural bridge** of lofted rock crosses the lake from the shore to a dry shelf on the west wall. Its deck arches 0.8 m, with 1.05 m of air between its underside and the water.
- **The falls** come through a swallow hole in the far dome and fall about 20 m into the pool beyond the shelf, as five ribbons that spread as they fall, with foam and mist. The shaft's funnel now starts just under the roof, so it no longer hangs below the ceiling like a cap.
- **The dressing:**
  - five columns, floor to roof, waisted and fluted, two of them standing in the lake;
  - stalactites in 34 clusters, lumpy rather than cones, every tip 3 m or more over the floor beneath it;
  - stalagmites with blunt tops, under a third of the stalactites over dry ground and scattered on the shore;
  - 16 flowstone curtains with V-shaped, scalloped hems, hung from the overhangs;
  - 22 fallen blocks, made from noisy icosahedra (the rounded boxes read as luggage);
  - the glowing flowers, now by the pools.
- **The view:** `places.html?place=cave` keeps `lake` (now from the ledge, the reveal), `shore` (from the ramp's foot), `falls` (from the shelf) and `passage`, and adds `bridge`. The light is the day down the shaft (Michael's A), a wide cool bounce off the white water, the flowers, and your torch. The first pass was far too bright, more like day than a cave, and the ambient and the bounce were cut by half.

- **Is this the measure?** At 64 by 46 by 26 m it is a great cavern, not a typical one. If Michael means caves to be this size as a rule, the lair (#314, next) and the mine follow. If not, `RX`, `RY` and `L` scale it down. The Old Gates' own size is card F5's (deep work).

## v80 — Session 861 — Flippers in the kit: a sea turtle and the maw turtle (backlog L3, prototype only)
Session 854 left the turtles owed from OG-016 and OG-084, because the kit had no flipper. Under FREEZE #297 this run works only in the prototypes, so this is the kit and two plans in `creatures.js`, and the sea is now twenty-two.

**The flipper.** It is not a new part. It is the kit's arm with two small additions. `s` flattens the arm's flesh, the same per-axis scale the spine and tail already take, so a three-bone arm squashed to 0.3 of its height becomes a paddle. `stroke` makes the pose beat it as a turtle flies through water: down and up about the body's long axis, swept back on the downstroke, feathered on the way up. The upstroke is held to 0.55 of the downstroke so the flipper does not rise through the shell's edge. The swim gait beats it once a stride. Standing, it beats at a quarter of the swim's amplitude, a slow paddle. Arms with no `stroke` swing as before. Their flesh takes `s` only when a plan gives one, and no existing plan does, so nothing else changes.

- **Sea turtle:** the tortoise's low body, widened (spine scaled 2 across, 0.6 high), under a flatter shell (1.05 m long, 0.92 wide, 0.26 high, scutes 0.2 m). It has a short neck and a blunt head. The front flippers are 0.64 m and beat together; the rear ones are 0.3 m, a half-stride behind, and mostly steer. The spine's wave is nearly off (0.015), so the shell stays still while the flippers work. Its hide is olive with darker patches and its shell red-brown. It swims at 0.45 body lengths a second.
- **Maw Turtle:** OG-016's deep and legendary turtle that "carries an ecosystem on its back". It is the same turtle at 11 times the size, about 11.5 m of shell. The shell is a greyer, rougher stone, with the Mossback's garden on top: 70 tufts of green-blue weed and 90 coral-red and pale blooms. Its water line (0.62) puts the garden above the surface, so from a deck it is a reef island until it moves. It swims at 0.08 body lengths a second.

Both set the flesh grid's cell to 0.016. Left to itself, the kit sizes the cell from the thinnest flesh, which is the flattened flipper (0.0095 m). The first build of the sea turtle came out at 106,876 triangles for that reason.
### Verified (headless Chromium)
- **`creatures.check.mjs`: all 799 checks pass** across 104 plans, with the sea check now counting twenty-two.
  - The sea turtle builds in 0.62 s, with 25 bones and 26,168 triangles; the maw turtle in 0.53 s, with 25 bones and 26,340 triangles.
  - Every skin weight sums to one, and both genomes are 153 and 155 bytes.
- **Speeds:** the sea turtle swims at 0.75 m/s, and the maw turtle at 1.39.
- **Pictures:** `creatures-seaturtle.jpg`, `creatures-mawturtle.jpg` and their `-bones` pictures. The first shots showed the front flipper raised through the shell's front edge and a pale band where the shell's rim overhung a narrow body. The flipper's root was moved forward and out, the upstroke shortened and the body widened, and the second shots show neither.
### Needs eyes
- **The flippers are flat paddles of even thickness.** A real turtle's front flipper is long and curved like a wing, with a scaled leading edge. A tapered outline would want a fin-like sheet with skin, which the kit does not have.
- **The maw turtle's garden** is the Mossback's land garden recoloured as weed and coral. A reef wants kelp that streams and barnacled rock, and the shell has no rock lumps of its own.
- **The bestiary's water plane** does not show in these stills, which matches the other swimmers' pictures.

## v80 — Session 862 — A coiled shell in the kit: the pierwinkle (backlog L3, prototype only)
The pierwinkle is OG-016's tide-pool snail, drawn there in purple beside the tidecrab. Session 856 left it owed because the kit had no coiled shell. This adds the part (`coil` in `creatures.js`) and the plan, and the sea is now twenty-three. It is prototype only, under FREEZE #297.

**The coil.** A tube is wound round an axis and grows as it goes, so its whorls stack into a spire. Toward the apex it shrinks by `grow` each turn (1.9 here) and rises toward `spire`; at the mouth it is widest. The colours are vertex colours:
- spiral bands run along the whorls (`bands`, three per round of the tube) in the plan's `band` tone;
- the sutures, where one whorl sits on the last, are darkened;
- the lip at the mouth is paled toward the belly.

It is one rigid mesh on a spine bone. `tilt`, `turn` and `roll` set it on the body: here it leans back 60° over the foot, turned so the mouth faces down and back onto it. Four turns at 40 steps a turn by 20 round make 6,400 triangles.

**Pierwinkle:** a broad flat foot on four spine bones that tapers to a point behind, a short neck, a head with two dark eye stalks (the Tidecrab's), and the shell. The shell is purple with pale pink bands and dark sutures. The snail is built at ten times its size and scaled by 0.16, so it is about 8 cm long. It creeps at a tenth of its length a second.
### Verified (headless Chromium)
- **`creatures.check.mjs`: all 804 checks pass** across 105 plans, with the sea check now counting twenty-three.
- **The build:** the pierwinkle builds in 0.25 s, with 6 bones and 14,552 triangles; its skin weights sum to one and its genome is 156 bytes. A first build with three spine bones (5 in all) failed the kit's "more than five bones" check, so the foot has four.
- **Pictures:**
  - `creatures-pierwinkle.jpg` is at its true size beside the figure, a speck.
  - `creatures-pierwinkle-close.jpg` (side) and `-close-front.jpg` were shot at ten times its size to show the shell. The first close shot had a plain shell, with the bands too faint against the purple; the bands were made pale and sharp.
### Needs eyes
- **The mouth of the shell is the tube's open end.** It has no flared lip or operculum, and from the front the open ring shows beside the head.
- **The coil is smooth.** A periwinkle's shell has fine growth lines across the whorls, which the vertex colours do not draw.
- **The kelpstrider** (a leafy seahorse) still waits for a frond part.

## v80 — Session 863 — Leafy fronds in the kit: the kelpstrider (backlog L3, prototype only)
The kelpstrider was the last of OG-016's twenty sea animals still owed: a leafy seahorse of the kelp forests. It needed a part the kit lacked. This adds `fronds` to `creatures.js` and the plan, and the sea is now twenty-four. Every animal on OG-016 is now a plan. It is prototype only, under FREEZE #297.

**The fronds.** They are lobed leaves hung off a body's bones. `n` of them are spread down the chains named in `on` (here the head, the neck, the spine and the tail), alternating sides. Each leans out (`out`), back (`back`) and up or down (`spread`), with its length, width and lean seeded by the genome. A frond is a twelve-point outline with two notches in each edge, coloured from the `frond` tone at its root to `frondTip` at its end. Each is a sheet skinned to its bone, so it sways as the body moves. The leaf's plane is set across the body's side, so the leaves face a side view rather than showing their edges. The first pictures had the leaves lying flat and seen edge-on.

**Kelpstrider:** the body stands upright on four spine bones (the hip low, the chest high, a slight hollow in front). The neck turns the head forward through 90°, and the head has a long tube snout. The tail curls forward under it on six bones. It has a small fluttering fin on its back and twenty-eight fronds. It is yellow-olive, mottled, with green fronds yellowing to their tips. It is about 30 cm tall and swims upright at 0.15 of its length a second.
### Verified (headless Chromium)
- **`creatures.check.mjs`: all 809 checks pass** across 106 plans, with the sea check now counting twenty-four.
- **The build:** the kelpstrider builds in 0.1 to 0.2 s, with 14 bones and 8,276 triangles of flesh, at a flesh cell of 0.004 for its thin snout. Its skin weights sum to one and its genome is 155 bytes.
- **Pictures:** `creatures-kelpstrider.jpg` (side) and `creatures-kelpstrider-front.jpg`. A first pass with a banded coat drew vertical stripes on the upright body, like a melon, so the coat is mottled instead.
### Needs eyes
- **The fronds all lean back,** so the leaves stand along its back and tail like a crest. A leafy sea dragon also trails them from its belly and snout.
- **The leaves are flat cards** with no veins and no transparency at their edges.
- **The swim** is the kit's spine wave turned to the vertical plane. A seahorse swims by fluttering its back fin and holding its body still, so the wave may be too much.

## v80 — Session 864 — A moth's glass wings: the Glasswing Moth, the last of Aurenne's fifteen (backlog L3, prototype only)
OG-030 draws the Glasswing Moth in oases and ruins, with crystalline wings, drawn to moonlight and flowering plants: a night ingredient. Session 848 left it owed, because the kit had no insect's wing. It is now a plan in `creatures.js`, so all fifteen of `AURENNE` are plans. It is prototype only, under FREEZE #297.

**The wings** are the kit's fins (Session 774), with three small additions:
- **Two outlines in `FIN`:** `fore`, pointed at the tip, and `hind`, rounded.
- **A fin role, `wing`.** At rest it holds the wing half-raised, 0.28 rad, breathing. In the air it beats twice a stride, from 0.1 down to 0.9 rad up.
- **A plan field, `finRough`,** for the sheets' roughness. The moth's is 0.08 against the default 0.5, so the wings shine like glass. At an opacity of 0.38 they are clear and faintly blue. The kit's per-vertex tint jitter on each sheet reads as facets.

No other plan sets either field, so nothing else changes.

**Flight** needed one change to the legs. Aloft, the kit tucks every foot up and back as a bird does. An insect's splayed legs (the presets with `yaw`) cannot reach that target: the first try missed by 7.9 cm, and pulling the feet in under the body still missed by 9.5 cm. Now an insect's legs only draw in a quarter of the way and hang a little below their standing reach. Every other soaring plan has bird legs, so none changes.

**Glasswing Moth:** a cream, furry body (three spine bones, the abdomen tapering to a point), a round head with large dark eyes, and two thin antennae swept forward and up. It has six insect legs and four glass wings: forewings 0.42 by 0.72 of its own length and hindwings 0.36 by 0.5. It is built at ten times its size and scaled by 0.1, so it is about 6 cm long with a span near 15 cm. It walks, flies and stands. Its flesh cell is set to 0.01; without that, the thin legs drove its first build to 60,304 triangles.
### Verified (headless Chromium)
- **`creatures.check.mjs`: all 816 checks pass** across 107 plans, and Aurenne's check now asks for fifteen.
- **The build:** the moth builds in 0.26 to 0.33 s, with 38 bones and 11,796 triangles. Its skin weights sum to one and its genome is 158 bytes.
- **Gaits:** walking, its feet are down 0.71 of the stride against a duty of 0.68. Every foot reaches its target in all three gaits.
- **Pictures:**
  - `creatures-glasswingmoth.jpg` is at its true size.
  - `-close-top.jpg` and `-close-soar.jpg` were shot at ten times its size. The first true-size shot showed the wings too small for a moth, so both pairs were made about 40% larger.
### Needs eyes
- **The wings are plain glass.** They have no veins, and the crystal is only the tint's facets. OG-030's wings "resonate with ambient magic", which a faint glow at night could carry; the kit's glow is for flesh, not sheets.
- **In flight its legs hang** rather than fold, which is right for a moth but reads long in the close picture.
- **The antennae are thin tapered horns,** not a moth's feathered ones.

## v80 — Session 865 — The common set by island: one body, three coats (backlog L3, prototype only)
OG-084 calls its ten animals of all islands "the shared base set that can be built once and recoloured". Session 843 built them once, and the recolouring was owed. It is prototype only, under FREEZE #297.

**How.** A creature's genome may now carry an `island` (`gatelands`, `mark` or `aurenne`). When it does, the plan's palette takes that island's coat from `COATS` in `creatures.js` over its own. The bones and the flesh are the same. The ten plans are the Gatelands' coats, the temperate middle. The Mark's run colder, greyer and paler, and Aurenne's sandier and warmer, as animals' coats do with climate:
- **The Mark:** a grey-white wolf; a cross fox with a dark saddle; a grey mountain hare; the hooded crow, grey-bodied with black wings; a near-black boar; a greyer deer, badger and otter; a silver sea-run trout.
- **Aurenne:** a sandy, jackal-pale wolf; a pale sand-red fox; a sandy hare; a brown-necked crow; a paler boar and deer; a pale grey badger; a lighter otter; a golden trout.
- **The raven** is black on every island and has no entry.

**The saved genome.** `toSaved` writes the island only when a genome has one, so every saved genome before this reads and writes as it did. `fromSaved` takes the island back if it is one of the three and drops anything else.

**The bestiary** reads `?isle=` in both its views. The check's `--sheet` now carries `--q` into the line shot, and a new `--sheet-only` skips the single shots.
### Verified (headless Chromium)
- **`creatures.check.mjs`: all 837 checks pass**, 21 of them new.
  - Each common animal built for the Mark and for Aurenne has the same number of bones as its Gatelands build.
  - Each recoloured one's mean vertex colour moved by 0.026 (the Markish boar, darker on dark) to 0.246 (the Markish wolf).
  - The raven moved 0.
  - The island survives `toSaved` → JSON → `fromSaved`. A genome with no island, or with `atlantis`, carries none.
- **The crow:** the first Aurennais crow moved only 0.012, because its black flight feathers are sheets and the check reads the flesh. Its body was browned until it moved 0.053.
- **Pictures:** `creatures-common-mark.jpg` and `creatures-common-aurenne.jpg`, the ten in a line beside the figure, against Session 843's `creatures-common.jpg`. The first Aurenne sheet had a bright orange deer and a yellow-green wolf, and both were toned down.
### Needs eyes
- **The line's per-animal hue jitter** (each genome's `tint`, ±0.05) still pulls the Aurennais deer toward red and the wolf toward olive, as it pulled the Gatelands' wolf olive in Session 843.
- **Coat is all that changes.** A northern hare would also be bigger with shorter ears, and a desert fox would have larger ears. Those are slider changes the island could carry later.
